teile.einleitung: The degree Fahrenheit is a unit of temperature used mainly in the USA. The freezing point of water is at 32 °F, the boiling point at 212 °F. The scale was invented by the physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1724.
wichtigste: The Fahrenheit scale was proposed by Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1724.
0 °C equals 32 °F, and 100 °C equals 212 °F.
You convert Celsius into Fahrenheit by multiplying by 1.8 and adding 32.
20 °C is 68 °F, and 50 °F is 10 °C.
At minus 40 degrees the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same value.
The normal body temperature of 37 °C equals 98.6 °F.
Fahrenheit fixed the zero point with a freezing mixture of ice, water and sal ammoniac.

abschnitte.text: The **degree Fahrenheit**, abbreviated °F, is a unit of temperature like the degree Celsius. Between the freezing point of water at 32 °F and the boiling point at 212 °F there are 180 Fahrenheit degrees. In Celsius there are only 100 degrees, which is why a Fahrenheit degree is smaller. One degree Celsius equals 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit.

**Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit** was born in Danzig in 1686 and died in The Hague in 1736. He built very accurate thermometers and was one of the first to use mercury in them. In 1724 he proposed his temperature scale. He fixed the zero point with a **freezing mixture** of ice, water and sal ammoniac, the coldest temperature he could produce in the laboratory at that time.

To convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit: multiply by 1.8 and add 32. So 20 °C is exactly 68 °F and 37 °C exactly 98.6 °F. The other way round, you first subtract 32 and then divide by 1.8, so 50 °F becomes exactly 10 °C. At **minus 40 degrees** both scales are the same; this is the only such point.

Today it is mainly the **USA** that uses degrees Fahrenheit in everyday life, for example in the weather forecast or when baking. Some smaller countries in the Caribbean and the Pacific also use it. Most countries in the world, including Switzerland, measure temperature in degrees Celsius. In science people calculate with **kelvin**, where 0 kelvin is absolute zero at minus 273.15 °C.

Anyone travelling to the USA should know the rule of thumb: values around 70 °F feel pleasantly warm. At 32 °F it freezes, and above 90 °F it is very hot. A fever of 104 °F equals 40 °C. Many oven recipes from America give temperatures such as 350 °F, which is about 175 °C.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed system of numbers used to measure how warm or cold something is.
The temperature at which water turns into ice: 0 °C or 32 °F.
The temperature at which water boils: 100 °C or 212 °F at sea level.
A mixture, for example of ice and salt, that gets colder than pure ice.
The unit of temperature in science, which starts at absolute zero.

gewusst: At minus 40 degrees it makes no difference whether you say Celsius or Fahrenheit; both show the same number.
Fahrenheit was originally a merchant and taught himself how to make measuring instruments.
The Celsius scale was proposed only about 20 years after the Fahrenheit scale.

teile.einleitung: The gram is a unit of mass used to weigh light things. One gram is a thousandth of a kilogram, which is very little: a paper clip weighs about that much. The symbol for gram is a small g.
wichtigste: The gram is a unit of mass, abbreviated g.
1000 grams make 1 kilogram.
A paper clip weighs about one gram.
A standard bar of chocolate weighs 100 grams.
A five-franc coin weighs about 13 grams.
One millilitre of water weighs about one gram.
Very small masses are measured in milligrams, a thousandth of a gram.

abschnitte.text: The **gram** is a unit of mass, that is of how heavy something is. It is a thousandth of a **kilogram**, which is the base unit in the International System of Units. So 1000 grams are 1 kilogram, which is why 1 kilogram is more than 900 grams. The word comes from the Greek gramma, which originally meant a small weight.

The gram was introduced in France at the end of the 18th century, when the metric system was invented. At that time it was decided that one gram is the mass of one cubic centimetre of **water** at the temperature of melting ice. That is why a millilitre of water still weighs about one gram today. A litre of water accordingly weighs about one kilogram.

A paper clip weighs about 1 gram, a sheet of A4 printer paper about 5 grams. A Fünfliber, the five-franc coin, weighs about 13 grams. A standard **bar of chocolate** has 100 grams, a hen's egg about 60 grams. Two packets of butter of 250 grams each make 500 grams together, which in Switzerland is a pound.

Many small animals are weighed in grams, for example a **mouse**, which often weighs only 20 to 30 grams. The smallest hummingbirds weigh only about 2 grams. An ant weighs much less than a gram, often only a few **milligrams**. That is why it would take hundreds of ants to make a single gram.

On food it says how many grams are in the packet, for example 500 g of pasta. The nutrition table usually shows how much sugar, fat and protein there is in **100 grams**. This makes it easy to compare different products. When baking, too, you weigh out flour and sugar in grams with kitchen scales.

A **milligram** is a thousandth of a gram, a microgram a millionth of a gram. The active ingredient in medicines, for example, is given in these units. For gemstones the carat is used; one carat equals 0.2 grams. Gold and silver are often traded in grams, because even small amounts cost a lot of money.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity that shows how much matter a body has and how heavy it is.
1000 grams, the base unit of mass.
A thousandth of a gram.
A device used to determine mass.

gewusst: A five-franc coin weighs about as much as thirteen paper clips together.
In everyday life in Switzerland, a pound means 500 grams.
A single grain of rice weighs only about a fiftieth of a gram.

teile.einleitung: Isotopes are different kinds of atoms of the same chemical element. They have the same number of protons in the nucleus but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different weights. Some isotopes are stable; others decay and give off radiation as they do so.
wichtigste: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Isotopes whose nuclei do not decay are called stable isotopes.
Carbon-12 is by far the most common isotope of carbon.
Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons and is radioactive.
Archaeologists use carbon-14 to work out the age of finds.
Deuterium is hydrogen with one proton and one neutron; tritium has two neutrons.
With ten stable isotopes, tin has the most of all the elements.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a nucleus made of **protons** and **neutrons**. The number of protons decides which element it is: carbon always has 6 protons. But the number of neutrons can vary, and this creates different **isotopes**. They are named after the total number of particles in the nucleus, for example carbon-12 or carbon-14.

The word isotope comes from Greek and means same place. This refers to the fact that all isotopes of an element are in the same place in the periodic table. The term was coined by the British chemist **Frederick Soddy** in 1913. With a mass spectrometer, isotopes can be separated by their mass and measured precisely.

Isotopes whose nuclei do not decay are called **stable isotopes**. Other isotopes are unstable and decay over time; they are radioactive. Carbon-12 makes up almost 99 per cent of natural carbon and is stable. Carbon-14, with 6 protons and 8 neutrons, on the other hand, is radioactive and occurs only in tiny amounts. With ten naturally occurring stable isotopes, tin holds the record among the elements.

Ordinary hydrogen has just one proton and no neutron. The isotope with one proton and one neutron is called **deuterium**, and it is twice as heavy. Water made from deuterium is called heavy water. The isotope with two neutrons is called tritium; it is radioactive and is used, for example, in self-luminous watch hands.

Living things take in carbon throughout their lives, including a little carbon-14. After death this isotope slowly decays, and its amount halves in about 5730 years. By measuring how much is left, you can work out the age of bones, wood or remains of cloth. This **radiocarbon method** was developed by the American Willard Libby, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1960.

In nuclear power stations such as Gösgen, the isotope **uranium-235** is split; it makes up only about 0.7 per cent of natural uranium. In medicine, radioactive isotopes help make organs visible or treat diseases, for example iodine-131 for the thyroid. Researchers study isotopes in ice cores to find out about the climate of past times. The age of the Earth was also worked out with isotopes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
Particle with no charge in the atomic nucleus.
Substance made of atoms with the same number of protons, for example gold or oxygen.
Table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.

gewusst: Heavy water looks like normal water, but an ice cube made from it sinks to the bottom in ordinary water.
Using isotopes in tooth enamel, researchers can find out in which area a person grew up thousands of years ago.
Of the 118 known elements, only about 80 have any stable isotopes at all.

teile.einleitung: The calorie is an old unit of energy, especially of heat. Today we come across it almost only on food packaging, where it shows how much energy a food gives the body. The official unit of energy, however, is the joule.
wichtigste: Originally a calorie was the energy that warms 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius.
When people talk about “calories” in everyday life, they usually mean kilocalories.
One kilocalorie is 1000 calories and equals about 4.2 kilojoules.
The calorie is not an SI unit; the SI unit of energy is the joule.
One gram of fat provides about 9 kilocalories.
One gram of protein or carbohydrate provides about 4 kilocalories.
Swiss food usually shows both figures, kilojoules and kilocalories.

abschnitte.text: The word **calorie** comes from the Latin “calor”, which means heat. Originally a calorie was the amount of heat needed to warm 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius. This amount is very small, so people usually work with the **kilocalorie**, abbreviated kcal. One kilocalorie warms a whole litre of water by 1 degree. When a packet or a conversation mentions “calories”, it almost always means kilocalories.

In the international system of units, the **SI**, energy is measured in **joules**, named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule. One kilocalorie equals 4.184 kilojoules, or about 4.2 kJ. A yoghurt with 100 kcal therefore provides about 420 kJ. Because the joule applies to all forms of energy, such as electricity, movement and heat, everything can easily be compared with it. That is why the calorie is hardly used in science and technology any more.

The body gets energy from three **nutrients**: fat, protein and carbohydrates. One gram of fat provides about 9 kcal, and one gram of protein or carbohydrate about 4 kcal each. A snack with 20 grams of fat therefore provides about 180 kcal from the fat alone. The 7 grams of protein in a glass of milk provide about 28 kcal. You can read such figures in the **nutrition table** on a packet.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs energy for
abschnitte.text: The body needs energy all the time, even when asleep, for example for the heartbeat, breathing and keeping a steady body temperature. This basic need is called the **basal metabolic rate**. Anyone who moves, does sport or is growing needs extra energy. Children and teenagers need a lot of energy because their bodies are still growing. What matters is not just the amount but also a balanced diet with vegetables, fruit and wholegrain products.

The energy content of a food can be measured with a **calorimeter**. A small sample is burnt in a closed container surrounded by water. From how much the water warms up, you calculate how much energy was in the sample. Today the figures on packets are usually calculated from the amount of fat, protein and carbohydrates. The figures are often given per 100 grams and sometimes also per portion.

begriffe.erklaerung: 1000 calories, abbreviated kcal, the usual figure on food.
The official unit of energy in the international system of units.
The energy the body needs at complete rest for its life processes.
A measuring device used to find out how much heat is released in a process.

gewusst: The energy in a bar of chocolate would be enough to bring several litres of cold water to the boil.
Water also has a place in the nutrition table, but it provides zero kilocalories.
One gram of fat provides more than twice as much energy as one gram of sugar.

teile.einleitung: An igloo is a dome-shaped house made of snow blocks. Traditionally the Inuit in the Arctic built igloos as shelter for the winter or for hunting trips. Although it is made of snow, it is much warmer inside than outside in the icy wind.
wichtigste: An igloo is a snow hut shaped like a dome.
Traditionally the Inuit in Canada and Greenland built igloos.
The blocks are best cut from firm, compacted snow.
Snow contains a lot of air and therefore insulates very well.
The inside is warmed mainly by the body heat of the people.
The entrance is small and low so that little heat escapes.
Inside it is only a little warmer than zero degrees, so the igloo does not melt away.

abschnitte.text: The word **igloo** comes from the language of the Inuit and simply means house. In English, though, it means the round hut made of snow. The **Inuit** live in the cold regions of northern Canada, Alaska and Greenland. In the past, hunters on the move built an igloo in a few hours to spend the night in it. Today the Inuit live in permanent houses but still know how to build igloos.

With a long knife or a saw you cut blocks from firm **snow** that has been compacted by the wind. Loose powder snow is no good because it crumbles. The blocks are stacked in a spiral that gets narrower towards the top. This creates a **dome** that supports itself without any props. Gaps are filled with snow, and a small air hole is often left at the top.

Snow consists largely of trapped air, and air conducts heat poorly. That is why the snow wall acts like thick **insulation**, rather like a down jacket. The body heat of the people and sometimes a small blubber lamp heat the room. Outside it can be minus 30 degrees, while inside it often stays around zero degrees. Because it hardly gets above zero inside, the wall melts slightly at the surface at most and then freezes into a smooth, solid layer of ice.

The entrance is a low tunnel that lies lower than the living space. Warm air rises and cold air sinks. The cold air therefore stays trapped in the low entrance as if in a **cold trap**. The sleeping places are on a raised snow bench, where the warmest air is. Furs on the bench give extra protection from the cold below.

In the Swiss Alps, too, mountaineers, scouts and families build igloos, whether for fun or as emergency shelter. Some ski areas have igloo villages in winter where guests can even spend the night. To build your own igloo you need enough firm snow, patience and ideally experienced helpers. An **air hole** is always important so that enough fresh air gets in.

begriffe.erklaerung: A people who live in the cold regions of Canada, Alaska and Greenland.
A round, curved roof that looks like half a ball.
A layer that stops heat or cold from getting through.
A low spot where heavy, cold air collects.

gewusst: A skilled Inuit hunter could build a small igloo in about an hour.
An igloo dome is so stable that an adult can often stand on it.
In the language of the Inuit, the word igloo simply means house.

teile.einleitung: The joule is the unit used to measure energy, work and heat. Whether you lift a bar of chocolate, make a lamp shine or heat water, the energy can always be given in joules. The unit is named after the English scientist James Prescott Joule.
wichtigste: The joule (symbol J) is the unit of energy, work and heat in the International System of Units.
One joule is the work done by a force of 1 newton over a distance of 1 metre.
One joule is exactly the same as one watt second.
To lift a 100 g bar of chocolate one metre you need about 1 joule.
Power is not measured in joules but in watts.
James Prescott Joule showed that mechanical work can be turned into heat.
1000 joules are one kilojoule, a million joules are one megajoule.

abschnitte.text: The **joule** is the unit of energy. Energy is found in movement, in heat, in light, in electric current and in food. Because energy can be turned from one form into another, all these forms are measured with the same unit. The symbol for the joule is a capital J.

In physics you do **work** when a force moves something over a distance. You calculate force times distance: 1 newton times 1 metre gives 1 joule. If you push a box with 50 newtons for 4 metres, you do 50 times 4, or 200 joules of work. A 100 g bar of chocolate weighs about 1 newton, so you need about 1 joule to lift it one metre.

**Power** tells you how much energy is converted per second and is measured in watts. One watt means 1 joule per second, so 1 joule is the same as one **watt second**. A 10 watt LED lamp therefore uses 10 times 60, or 600 joules, in one minute. The electricity bill shows kilowatt hours; one kilowatt hour equals 3.6 million joules or 3.6 megajoules.

On food packaging you find the energy content in **kilojoules** (kJ) and also in kilocalories. One kilocalorie equals about 4.2 kilojoules. A bar of chocolate contains more than 2000 kilojoules, in other words more than two million joules. This shows that a single joule is quite a small amount of energy.

**James Prescott Joule** lived from 1818 to 1889 in England and came from a brewing family. In famous experiments he let a falling weight turn a paddle wheel in a container of water. He measured that the water warmed up a tiny bit. In this way he showed that mechanical work can be turned into heat and that energy is not lost.

For large amounts of energy, prefixes are used. One kilojoule is 1000 joules, so 2.5 kilojoules are exactly 2500 joules. One **megajoule** is a million joules or 1000 kilojoules, so 3.6 megajoules equal 3600 kilojoules. For very large amounts there are also gigajoules and terajoules.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to move something, heat it or make it shine.
Force times distance, the energy you use when moving something.
Energy that a 1 watt device uses in one second, exactly 1 joule.
1000 joules, often given on food packaging.

gewusst: If you climb one storey of about 3 metres and weigh 40 kilograms, you already do about 1200 joules of work.
The old energy unit, the calorie, is no longer used in physics today, but it is still given on food.
Joule is even said to have tried to measure the temperature difference between the top and bottom of a waterfall on his honeymoon.

teile.einleitung: An insulator is a material that does not conduct electric current, or hardly at all. Insulators protect us from electric shocks; one example is the plastic sheath around a cable. In electrical engineering, the porcelain or glass parts from which power lines hang are also called insulators.
wichtigste: Insulators are materials that do not conduct electric current.
Examples are plastic, rubber, glass, porcelain, dry wood and dry air.
The plastic sheath of a cable stops current flowing into your hand.
In insulators there are almost no freely moving charge carriers.
At very high voltage even an insulator can break down.
On pylons the lines hang from insulators made of porcelain, glass or plastic.
Water with dissolved substances conducts electricity, which is why wet hands are dangerous.

abschnitte.text: An **insulator** is the opposite of a conductor. In metals such as copper, electrons can move freely and so carry current. In insulators the electrons are tightly bound to their atoms. That is why hardly any current can flow there.

Every cable consists of a copper wire in the middle and plastic **insulation** on the outside. Plugs, sockets and light switches also have plastic casings. Tools for electricians have insulated handles. Many devices carry a symbol of two squares, one inside the other, which stands for **double insulation**.

High-voltage lines carry voltages of several hundred thousand volts. To stop the current flowing down the pylon into the ground, the wires hang from long chains of porcelain, glass or plastic. These parts are also called insulators. Their ribbed shape makes the path along the surface longer, so that no current can creep along it when it rains.

Every insulator only holds up to a certain voltage. If this is exceeded, the current suddenly jumps through the material; this is called **breakdown**. Lightning is a breakdown through the air, which normally insulates well. Moisture and dirt can also weaken insulators.

Completely pure water conducts electricity very poorly. But tap water, sweat and sea water contain dissolved salts and therefore conduct well. That is why you must never use electrical devices with wet hands or in the bath. In Swiss bathrooms, **residual current devices** therefore provide protection by switching off the current in a flash when there is danger.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material that conducts current well, for example copper.
Protective covering made of non-conducting material.
Sudden flow of current through an insulator when the voltage is too high.
Tiny, negatively charged particle that carries current in conductors.

gewusst: Diamond is a very good electrical insulator but conducts heat better than copper.
Birds can sit on a power line because they touch only one wire and no current flows through them to the earth.
The first insulators for telegraph lines in the 19th century were often made of glass.

teile.einleitung: Inductance describes how strongly an electrical component, above all a coil, resists changes in current. When current flows through a coil, it builds up a magnetic field and stores energy in it. Inductance is measured in henries and is found in transformers, radios and induction hobs.
wichtigste: Inductance is given in the unit henry.
The unit is named after the American physicist Joseph Henry.
1 henry equals 1 volt times second per ampere.
If you double the number of turns of a coil, its inductance becomes four times as large.
An iron core greatly increases the inductance of a coil.
Coils connected in series without coupling add up their inductances.
A coil and a capacitor together form an oscillating circuit.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a wire, a magnetic field is created. If you wind the wire into a **coil**, this field becomes much stronger. If the current changes, the magnetic field changes too, and this produces a voltage in the coil itself that works against the change. This behaviour is called **self-induction**, and its strength is given by the inductance L.

For a long coil with air inside: L equals the magnetic constant times the number of turns squared times the cross-sectional area divided by the length. An air coil with 500 turns, a cross section of 4 cm² and a length of 20 cm therefore has about 0.63 millihenries. Because the **number of turns** is squared, L becomes four times as large when the number of turns is doubled. An **iron core** concentrates the magnetic field and often increases the inductance by a hundred to a thousand times.

The unit of inductance is the **henry**, abbreviated H. A coil has 1 henry if a change in current of 1 ampere per second produces a voltage of 1 volt. Therefore 1 H = 1 V · s/A. The unit honours the American Joseph Henry, who studied self-induction around 1830, at about the same time as Michael Faraday in England.

With alternating current a coil acts like a resistance, which is called **inductive reactance**. It is calculated as 2 times pi times frequency times inductance. A coil of 0.1 henries has about 31 ohms at the 50 hertz of our mains supply. The higher the frequency, the more strongly the coil holds back the current.

If you connect a coil to a **capacitor**, you get an oscillating circuit. In it the energy swings back and forth between the magnetic field of the coil and the electric field of the capacitor. With L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF it oscillates at about 1.6 kilohertz. Oscillating circuits like this select a particular station in radios.

Inductances are found in many devices. In **transformers** two coils are coupled by an iron core and so change the voltage, for example in chargers. An induction hob uses a coil to create a rapidly changing magnetic field that heats the bottom of the pan directly. If you suddenly switch off a large coil, self-induction can produce a spark.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wound-up wire that can produce a strong magnetic field.
A coil produces a voltage itself when its current changes.
The unit of inductance, named after Joseph Henry.
A circuit of a coil and a capacitor in which energy swings back and forth.
A device made of two coils that makes an alternating voltage larger or smaller.

gewusst: The ignition coil of a petrol engine uses induction to turn 12 volts into many thousands of volts for the spark plug.
Wireless chargers for mobile phones work with two coils that transfer energy through a magnetic field.
Even a straight piece of wire has a tiny inductance.

teile.einleitung: The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest space telescope ever built. It mainly observes infrared light and can therefore see the first galaxies after the Big Bang. It was built jointly by the space agencies NASA, ESA and CSA.
wichtigste: The telescope was launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket.
The main mirror is made up of 18 hexagonal segments.
It observes mainly in the infrared range.
The mirrors are coated with a thin layer of gold, because gold reflects infrared light well.
A sunshield made of five layers of foil protects the telescope from heat.
NASA, ESA and CSA built it together.
It can see the strongly redshifted light of the first galaxies.

abschnitte.text: The **James Webb Space Telescope**, JWST for short, is a huge telescope in space. It is regarded as the successor to the famous Hubble telescope. It was built by the American NASA, the European ESA and the Canadian CSA. It is named after James Webb, who led NASA in the 1960s.

The telescope was launched on **25 December 2021** on a European Ariane 5 rocket from the Kourou spaceport in French Guiana. Because it was too big for the rocket, it was folded up and only unfolded in space. It now orbits around the **Lagrange point L2**, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. The first colour images were published in July 2022.

The main mirror has a diameter of about 6.5 metres and is made up of 18 hexagonal **segments** of beryllium. They are coated with a very thin layer of gold, because gold reflects infrared light particularly well. Hubble's mirror, by contrast, was only 2.4 metres across. The larger a mirror is, the more light it collects and the fainter the objects you can see.

A huge **sunshield**, about the size of a tennis court, protects the telescope from the light and heat of the Sun, Earth and Moon. It consists of five very thin layers of foil. As a result the shaded side gets colder than minus 220 degrees Celsius. This cold is necessary because warm parts give off infrared radiation themselves and would disturb the measurements.

The universe is expanding, so the light of very distant galaxies is stretched on its long journey. Visible light turns into **infrared light**; this is called **redshift**. That is why only an infrared telescope can see the first galaxies after the Big Bang. Infrared also passes through clouds of dust in which new stars and planets are forming.

The telescope has already found very early galaxies whose light has been travelling for more than 13 billion years. It also studies the atmospheres of **exoplanets**, planets around other stars, and has found carbon dioxide there, for example. Researchers from Switzerland also worked on the MIRI instrument for the mid-infrared. Its pictures of nebulae and galaxies are among the most beautiful images of space.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light with a longer wavelength than red, invisible to us but felt as warmth.
Stretching of the light of distant galaxies by the expansion of the universe.
Place in space where a satellite travels round the Sun together with the Earth.
Planet that orbits a star other than the Sun.

gewusst: The gold layer on all the mirrors together weighs only about as much as a golf ball.
The telescope is so far away that, unlike Hubble, it cannot be repaired by astronauts.
Because the launch on the Ariane 5 was so precise, a lot of fuel was left over, which extends the possible lifetime of the telescope.

teile.einleitung: Ionising radiation is very high-energy radiation that can knock electrons out of atoms. It includes X-rays, gamma rays and particle radiation from radioactive substances. It is useful in medicine and technology but can damage cells, so good radiation protection is needed.
wichtigste: Ionising radiation has enough energy to ionise atoms and molecules, in other words to give them an electric charge.
Neutrons have no charge and ionise only indirectly through particles they knock into or create.
Radiation dose is measured in sieverts, often in millisieverts or microsieverts.
The effective dose takes into account that organs differ in how sensitive they are.
Deterministic damage only occurs above a threshold dose; stochastic damage such as cancer has no safe threshold.
A short whole-body dose of around 4 to 5 sieverts is fatal without treatment for about half of those affected.
The ALARA principle requires keeping the dose as low as reasonably achievable.

abschnitte.text: To ionise means to knock an electron out of an atom so that a charged **ion** is left behind. This takes a great deal of energy, more than visible light or radio waves have. **Alpha radiation**, beta radiation, gamma radiation and X-rays can do this directly. Neutron radiation has no charge and acts only indirectly, because it knocks other particles or triggers nuclear reactions.

Part of the radiation is completely natural and has always been there. It comes from space as **cosmic radiation**, from rocks in the ground and from the radioactive gas **radon**, which can collect in cellars. In Switzerland radon makes up the largest part of the radiation a person receives in a year. On top of that come artificial sources such as X-rays and CT scans at the doctor's.

The energy absorbed per kilogram of body tissue is called the **absorbed dose** and is measured in grays. Because alpha rays are more harmful than gamma rays, this is converted into the equivalent dose in **sieverts**. The effective dose also takes into account that bone marrow, for example, is more sensitive than skin. In Switzerland a person receives on average a few millisieverts a year, a large part of which comes from radon.

Radiation can damage the genetic material in cells. At very high doses **deterministic damage** occurs, for example acute radiation sickness, which only starts above a threshold and gets worse with the dose. At small doses the concern is **stochastic damage** such as cancer, whose likelihood rises with the dose. For this, radiation protection assumes a linear model without a threshold, to be on the safe side.

In radiation protection three simple rules apply: keep your **distance**, keep the time spent short and use shielding. Distance has a particularly strong effect, because with a point source the dose rate falls with the square of the distance. If you measure 90 microsieverts per hour at 2 metres, it is only 10 at 6 metres. Lead and thick concrete are good for shielding gamma rays, while even a sheet of paper stops alpha rays.

Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered the rays named after him (X-rays) in 1895, and Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896. Today X-rays are used to take pictures of bones and teeth. In **radiotherapy** cancer cells are destroyed in a targeted way. Food, syringes and dressings are also sterilised with radiation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Atom or molecule that is electrically charged because it has lost electrons or has too many.
Unit for the effect of radiation on humans.
Natural radioactive gas from the ground that can collect in houses.
Abbreviation for “as low as reasonably achievable”, a principle of radiation protection.

gewusst: On a long-haul flight you receive more cosmic radiation than on the ground, because the protective layer of air is thinner.
Bananas contain a tiny amount of radioactive potassium, but the dose is completely harmless.
Röntgen never patented his discovery, so that everyone could benefit from it.

teile.einleitung: Isaac Newton was an English physicist and mathematician who lived more than 300 years ago. He was the first to explain that the same force makes an apple fall to the ground and keeps the Moon in its orbit. Pupils still learn his laws of motion today.
wichtigste: Isaac Newton lived from 1643 to 1727 in England.
He was professor of mathematics at the University of Cambridge.
He explained gravity as a force with which all bodies attract each other.
He set out three basic laws of motion.
With a prism he showed that white light is made up of all the colours of the rainbow.
He improved the telescope by using a mirror instead of a lens.
Later he ran the Royal Mint in London.

abschnitte.text: Isaac Newton was born at the beginning of 1643 in **Woolsthorpe** in England and died in London in 1727. He studied at the University of **Cambridge** and became professor of mathematics there in 1669. He was a physicist, mathematician and astronomer all at once. He is regarded as one of the most important natural scientists in history.

According to the story, Newton saw an apple fall from a tree and wondered why it falls straight down. He realised that the same **gravity** acts on the apple and on the Moon. The Moon stays in its orbit because the Earth attracts it. Newton described this force in the **law of gravitation**, which he published in 1687 in his book “Principia”. The famous apple tree still stands in Woolsthorpe today.

The first law is called the **law of inertia**: a ball at rest stays where it is if nothing pushes it. The second law says that a larger force accelerates an object more strongly. The third law states **action equals reaction**: every force has an equal opposite force. That is why a balloon shoots forwards when air rushes out of the back.

Newton let sunlight pass through a triangular piece of glass, a **prism**. In this way he showed that white light is made up of all the colours of the rainbow. He also built a **reflecting telescope**, which works with a curved mirror instead of lenses. Telescopes like this are still used in astronomy today.

From 1696 Newton worked for the Royal **Mint** in London and later ran it. There he fought counterfeiters and made sure the coins were better. From 1703 he was President of the Royal Society, a famous society of scholars. He was buried in **Westminster Abbey** in London.

The unit of force is called the **newton** in his honour. His laws can be used to calculate how rockets fly and how bridges stay up. Newton also developed a new method of calculation, **calculus**, at almost the same time as the German Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Only Albert Einstein extended Newton's picture of gravity more than 200 years later.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force with which all bodies attract each other.
An object tends to stay as it is: at rest or in steady motion.
Triangular piece of glass that splits light into its colours.
Unit of force, abbreviated N.

gewusst: When the plague broke out in England, the university closed, and at home Newton had time for many of his most important ideas.
Newton was knighted and was therefore allowed to call himself “Sir Isaac Newton”.
Cuttings from Newton's apple tree now grow in gardens and universities all over the world.

teile.einleitung: The Grande Dixence is a huge dam in the canton of Valais and, at 285 metres, the tallest structure in Switzerland. It holds back the Lac des Dix, whose water is used to produce electricity. It is the tallest gravity dam in the world.
wichtigste: The Grande Dixence dam is 285 metres high.
It is the tallest structure in Switzerland and the tallest gravity dam in the world.
It was completed at the beginning of the 1960s, more than 60 years ago.
Behind the dam lies the Lac des Dix reservoir.
The water is used to produce electricity.
Through pumping stations and about 100 km of tunnels, water from other valleys as far as the Zermatt area reaches the lake.
French is spoken in the valley.

abschnitte.text: The Grande Dixence stands in the **Val des Dix**, a side valley of the Val d'Hérens in French-speaking Lower Valais. The top of the dam lies at about 2365 metres above sea level, right in the high mountains. From Sion you can reach it in summer by PostBus. All around are the peaks and glaciers of the Valais Alps. In winter the road to the dam is closed.

The dam was built from the early 1950s and was finished in 1961. At **285 metres** it is almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower without its aerial. The dam is about 700 metres long, 15 metres thick at the top and about 200 metres thick at the bottom. About 6 million cubic metres of **concrete** were needed to build it. With that you could build a wall 6000 kilometres long that is one metre high and one metre wide.

The Grande Dixence is a **gravity dam**. It withstands the water pressure by its enormous weight alone, rather like a giant wedge. At the bottom of the reservoir, at a water depth of 280 m, there is a **hydrostatic pressure** of about 27 bar. That is why the dam is much thicker at the bottom than at the top. Engineers constantly monitor whether the dam moves.

The **Lac des Dix** can store up to 400 million cubic metres of water. Most of the water comes from glaciers; there are 35 glaciers in its catchment area. Because its own streams are not enough, extra water is brought in from other valleys as far as the Zermatt area. For this there are pumping stations and about 100 km of **tunnels** through the mountains. In summer the lake fills with meltwater, and in winter it is emptied to produce electricity.

The water flows through tunnels and penstocks down into the Rhône valley to the power stations. There it drives **Pelton turbines**, which turn generators. When it went into operation at the end of the 1990s, the associated **Bieudron** power station held the world record for the greatest head of a hydroelectric power station, almost 1900 metres. One cubic metre of water falling 1000 m supplies about 2.7 kWh of energy. The plants produce valuable electricity for the whole of Switzerland, especially in winter.

The Grande Dixence is a popular place for an outing. In summer you can take a guided tour through the inside of the dam. A cable car takes you up to the top of the dam, from which you have an impressive view of the lake and down the valley. A hiking path runs along the shore of the lake to its far end.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wall that blocks off a valley and holds back water to form a lake.
A dam that holds back the water by its great weight alone.
An artificial lake behind a dam.
A passage through the mountain through which water flows.
The difference in height that the water falls down to the turbine.

gewusst: The dam weighs more than the Great Pyramid of Cheops in Egypt.
Before today's dam there was a smaller dam, the Dixence, which now lies sunk in the Lac des Dix.
The Lac des Dix is the largest reservoir in Switzerland by volume of water.

teile.einleitung: An interferometer is a measuring device that overlaps light waves to measure tiny differences in length. This produces bright and dark fringes that react even to shifts of a fraction of a wavelength. Huge interferometers have even detected the trembling of space itself, gravitational waves.
wichtigste: An interferometer splits a beam of light into two beams and later brings them together again.
The component that splits the beam is called a beam splitter.
Depending on the path length, the waves reinforce or cancel each other, creating bright and dark interference fringes.
If one light path gets longer by half a wavelength, bright and dark swap places.
In 1907 Albert Michelson became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Physics, partly for his interferometers.
The Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 found no evidence of a luminiferous ether.
The LIGO detectors, with arms 4 kilometres long, detected gravitational waves for the first time in 2015.

abschnitte.text: Light behaves like a wave with crests and troughs. When two waves meet so that crest falls on crest, they reinforce each other; this is called **constructive interference**. When crest falls on trough, they cancel out; this is **destructive interference**. You can see something similar when water waves from two stones cross in a pond.

In the best-known setup, light hits a **beam splitter**, a half-silvered mirror. One beam goes straight on to a mirror, the other sideways to a second mirror. Both are reflected back and brought together again at the beam splitter. If you move one mirror by 1 micrometre with a wavelength of 500 nanometres, 4 **interference fringes** pass by, because the light path there and back becomes twice as long.

In the **Mach-Zehnder interferometer** a beam of light is sent along separate paths with two beam splitters and two mirrors and brought together again at the end. It was described in 1891 and 1892 by Ludwig Zehnder and Ludwig Mach. The **Fabry-Pérot interferometer** consists of two parallel, partly mirrored surfaces between which the light travels back and forth many times. This lets it distinguish wavelengths very finely, and it is used in lasers, for example.

In the 19th century many researchers believed that light needed an invisible substance, the **luminiferous ether**, to travel through. In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley in the USA wanted to measure how the Earth moves through this ether. But their interferometer showed no difference, however it was turned. This result later helped Albert Einstein with his **theory of relativity** of 1905.

The two **LIGO** detectors in the US states of Washington and Louisiana are huge Michelson interferometers with arms 4 kilometres long. In September 2015 they recorded **gravitational waves** for the first time, coming from two merging black holes. The arms changed their length by less than a thousandth of the diameter of a proton. This discovery was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017.

In factories, interferometers check whether lenses and mirrors are ground perfectly smooth. In **precision measurement** they measure lengths to within nanometres. In fibre optic networks, components based on the Mach-Zehnder principle control the light signals. Radio telescopes are also linked together into interferometers to get sharper pictures of the sky.

begriffe.erklaerung: Overlapping of waves in which they reinforce or cancel each other.
Half-silvered mirror that divides a beam of light into two parts.
Distance from one wave crest to the next.
Invisible substance once thought to carry light. It does not exist.
Tiny distortion of space and time that spreads out like a wave.

gewusst: The LIGO interferometers are so sensitive that they even have to filter out passing lorries and ocean waves on the coast.
With his measurements Albert Michelson also determined the speed of light more accurately than anyone before him.
The shimmering colours of soap bubbles come from the same interference that an interferometer uses.

teile.einleitung: ITER is a huge experimental reactor with which researchers from all over the world want to show that energy can be obtained from nuclear fusion. It is being built in southern France and is meant to fuse atomic nuclei in a similar way to the Sun. The name refers to the Latin word “iter”, which means “the way”.
wichtigste: ITER is being built in France, at Cadarache near the town of Aix-en-Provence.
ITER is a fusion reactor of the tokamak type.
The aim is to produce ten times more fusion power than is put in to heat the plasma.
The plasma is meant to reach about 150 million degrees Celsius.
Superconducting magnet coils produce strong fields with almost no electrical losses.
The project is supported by 7 members (as of 2025).
ITER will not feed electricity into the public grid, because it is an experimental facility.

abschnitte.text: In the Sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones and release tremendous energy; this is called **nuclear fusion**. ITER is meant to fuse the hydrogen types **deuterium** and tritium into helium. This also produces fast neutrons, which give off their energy as heat. Unlike nuclear fission, it does not create long-lived radioactive fuel waste.

A **tokamak** is a ring-shaped chamber that looks like a giant doughnut. Inside it the gas becomes so hot that it turns into a **plasma**, in which electrons and atomic nuclei fly around separately. No material could withstand 150 million degrees, so strong magnetic fields keep the plasma away from the walls. The idea of the tokamak came from the Soviet Union in the 1950s.

ITER's magnet coils are made of **superconductors**, which conduct current without resistance. For this they have to be cooled with liquid helium to about minus 269 degrees. So right next to the hottest place on Earth is one of the coldest. The whole tokamak facility weighs about 23,000 tonnes, roughly as much as three Eiffel Towers.

The **European Union**, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA take part in ITER. The members supply many components from their own factories, which are then assembled in France. The agreement was signed in 2006, and building work on the site began soon afterwards. The timetable has had to be postponed several times; according to the 2024 plan, research operation is to start around 2034.

With about 50 megawatts of heating power, ITER is meant to produce about 500 megawatts of **fusion power**, ten times as much. If this succeeds, it would be an important step towards later fusion power stations that actually supply electricity. Such a power station, often called **DEMO**, is to be built only after ITER. One day fusion energy could provide a lot of electricity without greenhouse gases.

Nuclear fusion is also researched in Switzerland. The **Swiss Plasma Center** at EPFL in Lausanne has its own tokamak, called TCV. There researchers study which shape of plasma is most stable. Swiss companies and institutes have also supplied components and expertise for ITER.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fusing of light atomic nuclei, which releases a lot of energy.
Extremely hot gas in which electrons and atomic nuclei are separated.
Ring-shaped facility in which magnetic fields hold a hot plasma.
Material that, when very cold, conducts current with no resistance at all.
Heavy hydrogen, which is also found in sea water.

gewusst: The plasma in ITER is meant to become about ten times hotter than the inside of the Sun.
The word tokamak is a Russian abbreviation and means roughly “ring-shaped chamber with magnetic coils”.
Although the facility is huge, there are only a few grams of fuel in the plasma at any one time.

teile.einleitung: The degree Celsius, abbreviated °C, is the unit with which we measure temperature in Switzerland and almost everywhere in the world. At 0 °C water freezes, at 100 °C it boils. The unit is named after the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius.
wichtigste: The symbol °C stands for degree Celsius.
The unit is named after the Swede Anders Celsius.
Between the freezing point and the boiling point of water there are 100 equal parts.
Temperatures below 0 °C are written with a minus sign, for example -5 °C.
In the USA temperature is usually measured in degrees Fahrenheit in everyday life.
In science the unit kelvin is often used, where 0 °C equals 273.15 kelvin.
The lowest temperature at a Swiss weather station was measured in La Brévine in 1987: -41.8 °C.

abschnitte.text: The degree Celsius is a **unit of temperature**. The scale is fixed at two points for water: the **freezing point** at 0 °C and the **boiling point** at 100 °C, each at normal air pressure at sea level. In between it is divided into 100 equal parts. That is why it used to be called the centigrade scale. A thermometer shows the temperature in degrees Celsius.

**Anders Celsius** lived from 1701 to 1744 and was an astronomer at the University of Uppsala in Sweden. In 1742 he proposed a temperature scale with 100 parts. The surprising thing is that in his scale the boiling point was at 0 and the freezing point at 100. Only shortly after his death was the scale turned round so that higher numbers mean warmer. Celsius also studied the northern lights and took part in an expedition to Lapland.

If it is 8 °C in the morning and 15 °C in the afternoon, it has become 7 degrees warmer. With temperatures below zero you have to be careful: if the temperature rises from -6 °C to 9 °C, it becomes 15 degrees warmer. If it is 3 °C and it gets 5 degrees colder, the thermometer shows -2 °C. Of several temperatures below zero, the one with the smallest number after the minus is the warmest, so -5 °C is warmer than -25 °C. The average of -2 °C, 4 °C and 7 °C is calculated like this: 9 divided by 3 gives 3 °C.

In the USA **degrees Fahrenheit** are mostly used in everyday life. There water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F. In physics the unit **kelvin** is used, whose zero point is absolute zero. Absolute zero lies at -273.15 °C; it cannot get any colder. A difference of 1 kelvin is exactly as large as a difference of 1 degree Celsius.

The lowest temperature at a weather station in Switzerland was measured on 12 January 1987 in **La Brévine** in the Neuchâtel Jura: -41.8 °C. That is why the village is also called the Siberia of Switzerland. The highest temperature was measured in the heatwave summer of 2003 in **Grono** in the canton of the Grisons, at 41.5 °C. So there are more than 83 degrees between these two records. A person's body normally has a temperature of about 37 °C.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how warm or cold something is.
A measuring device for temperature.
The temperature at which water turns into ice, 0 °C.
The temperature at which water boils, 100 °C at sea level.
The physics unit of temperature, which starts at absolute zero.

gewusst: At -40 degrees a Celsius and a Fahrenheit thermometer show exactly the same number.
On the summit of Mount Everest water boils at only about 70 °C, because the air pressure there is much lower.
Originally, on Anders Celsius's scale, the boiling point was at 0 degrees.

teile.einleitung: Jacob Bernoulli was a mathematician from Basel who lived from 1655 to 1705. He is regarded as one of the founders of probability theory and belonged to the famous Bernoulli family of scholars from Basel. Many numbers, curves and equations still bear his name today.
wichtigste: Jacob Bernoulli was born in Basel in 1655 and was professor of mathematics at the University of Basel from 1687.
His main work on probability, the “Ars Conjectandi”, appeared in 1713 after his death.
He formulated a first version of the law of large numbers.
The Bernoulli numbers appear in sums of powers of natural numbers.
The figure-of-eight curve lying on its side called the lemniscate is named after him.
In 1690 he set the problem of finding the shape of a freely hanging rope, the catenary.
In 1697 he also solved the brachistochrone problem, whose solution is the cycloid.

abschnitte.text: Jacob Bernoulli was born in **Basel** in 1655, the son of a merchant family. His father wanted him to study theology, but Jacob secretly taught himself mathematics. After travelling to France, the Netherlands and England, he became a professor at the **University of Basel** in 1687. He died in Basel in 1705, and his gravestone stands in the cloister of Basel Minster.

Over several generations the Bernoullis produced important mathematicians and physicists. Jacob's younger brother **Johann Bernoulli** also became a famous mathematician. The two brothers often argued fiercely about who had found the better solution. Johann's son **Daniel Bernoulli** is known for the Bernoulli equation about flowing liquids.

In the **Ars Conjectandi**, which means “the art of conjecturing”, Jacob studied games of chance and random experiments. An experiment with only two outcomes, such as heads or tails, is called a **Bernoulli trial** today. The probability of getting exactly two heads in three coin tosses is 3/8. The probability of throwing a die four times without a single six is about 48 per cent.

Jacob proved that over a very large number of trials the relative frequency gets closer to the probability. This **law of large numbers** is one of the foundations of statistics. If you roll a die 60 times, you expect 10 sixes on average. The more often you roll, the closer the share of sixes comes to one sixth.

The **lemniscate** looks like a figure eight lying on its side and is used today as the infinity symbol. The **catenary** describes how a chain or rope hangs between two points. In the brachistochrone problem, people asked along which path a ball rolls fastest from one point to a lower one; the answer is the cycloid. Jacob also studied the logarithmic spiral, which fascinated him particularly.

The **Bernoulli numbers** play an important part in number theory and in working with series. The Bernoulli differential equation has the form y' + p(x)·y = q(x)·yⁿ and can be solved with a trick. While studying compound interest, Jacob came across a number that is known today as **Euler's number** e. Without his work there would be neither modern insurance nor weather forecasts with probabilities.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number between 0 and 1 that shows how certain it is that an event will happen.
Curve in the shape of a figure eight lying on its side.
Shape that a chain hung from two points takes on.
Path of a point on a rolling wheel.

gewusst: Jacob wanted a logarithmic spiral on his gravestone, but the stonemason mistakenly carved a different kind of spiral.
His gravestone bears the Latin motto “Eadem mutata resurgo”, which means “Though changed, I shall arise the same”.
The Bernoulli family produced at least eight well-known mathematicians.

teile.einleitung: A hydraulic press is a machine that uses a liquid to turn a small force into a huge force. It consists of two connected cylinders with pistons of different sizes. It is used to press sheet metal, forge metal or lift cars.
wichtigste: The increase in force comes from two pistons of different sizes.
The pressure in the liquid is the same under both pistons.
The forces are in the same ratio as the areas of the pistons.
With piston areas of 10 and 200 square centimetres, 50 newtons become a full 1000 newtons.
To gain force, the small piston has to travel a much longer distance.
Joseph Bramah patented the hydraulic press in England in 1795.
The hydraulic car jack uses the same principle.

abschnitte.text: A hydraulic press has two **cylinders** that are connected at the bottom by a pipe and filled with oil. One cylinder holds a small piston, the other a large one. When you push the small piston down, oil is forced into the large cylinder and lifts the large piston. A valve stops the oil from flowing back.

**Pressure** is force divided by area, and it is the same throughout the liquid. So the force on the small piston divided by its area equals the force on the large piston divided by its area. If the small piston has 10 square centimetres and the large one 200, the area is 20 times larger, and 50 newtons become 1000 newtons. The other way round, with 5 and 100 square centimetres you need only 100 newtons on the small piston to get 2000 newtons on the large one.

The press does not give you any energy for free. What you gain in force, you lose in **distance**: if the large piston is 20 times larger, it rises by only 1 centimetre when the small one is pushed down by 20 centimetres. The work, meaning force times distance, stays the same on both sides. This principle is called the **golden rule of mechanics** and also applies to levers and pulleys.

The English inventor Joseph Bramah patented the hydraulic press in 1795. He also invented a particularly secure lock and improved the flushing toilet. His press was based on Blaise Pascal's law about how pressure spreads in liquids. It became one of the most important machines of the Industrial Revolution.

In factories, giant presses shape car doors and roofs out of sheet steel. Scrap presses squash old cars into small cubes. Every garage has a hydraulic **car jack**, which lets you lift a car with little effort when changing a wheel. Hydraulic presses are also used to press fruit, oil seeds or waste paper.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a particular area.
Unit of force, abbreviated N.
Movable disc that slides up and down inside a cylinder.
Tool used to lift a car a little way.

gewusst: The largest hydraulic presses in the world reach forces of many tens of thousands of tonnes and forge aircraft parts in one piece.
With a small hydraulic car jack, even a child can lift a car a few centimetres.
The principle of the hydraulic press is based on a discovery by Blaise Pascal, after whom the unit of pressure is also named.

teile.einleitung: A gravitational field is the invisible area around every mass in which other masses are attracted. The Earth, the Moon and the Sun are surrounded by such fields. Because the gravitational field exists, apples fall to the ground and the Moon circles the Earth.
wichtigste: Every body with mass creates a gravitational field around it.
Gravitational field strength shows how strongly one kilogram of mass is attracted; its unit is N/kg.
At the Earth's surface the field strength is about 9.81 N/kg, on the Moon only about 1.6 N/kg.
The field lines of a sphere such as the Earth point radially towards its centre.
As the distance grows, the field strength decreases with the square of the distance.
At the poles the acceleration due to gravity is slightly greater than at the equator.
The surface of equal gravitational potential that roughly corresponds to mean sea level is called the geoid.

abschnitte.text: A **field** describes what force would act on a body at every place in space. In a gravitational field this is the attractive force of the mass. The **gravitational field strength** is the force per kilogram and is measured in N/kg. It is equal to the acceleration due to gravity g in m/s²; the two units mean the same thing. On Earth, therefore, a force of about 9.81 newtons acts on a body with a mass of 1 kg.

Physicists show fields with **field lines**, which show in which direction the force acts. In the gravitational field of a sphere they run **radially** towards the centre, like the spokes of a wheel. Where the lines are close together, the field is strong. Close to the Earth's surface, in a small area such as a room, the lines run almost parallel. This is then called a uniform field, which is equally strong everywhere.

In the 17th century Isaac Newton realised that the attraction decreases with the square of the distance from the centre. So twice the distance means only a quarter of the force. At a height of two Earth radii above the ground you are three times as far from the centre of the Earth, so the field strength there is only a ninth. The **gravitational potential** of a point mass M at a distance r is -G·M/r, if it is set to zero at infinity. Inside a hollow spherical shell of even thickness, all the attractions cancel out exactly, and the field strength there is zero.

The Earth is not a perfect sphere, but is slightly flattened at the poles. At the poles you are therefore a little closer to the centre of the Earth than at the equator. In addition, the Earth turns, and at the equator this produces a small **centrifugal force** outwards. Together, these mean that the acceleration due to gravity is about 9.83 m/s² at the poles and only about 9.78 m/s² at the equator. Mountain ranges such as the Alps and rock of different densities underground also change the gravitational field a little.

If you join up all the points with the same gravitational potential, you get an irregularly wavy surface, the **geoid**. It roughly corresponds to mean sea level, imagined as continuing under the continents. The geoid is important for giving heights, for example in the phrase “metres above sea level”. The Federal Office of Topography swisstopo calculates its own precise geoid model for Switzerland. Satellites such as GRACE have measured the gravitational field of the whole Earth.

In 1687 Newton described gravitation in his work “Principia” as a force between masses. Albert Einstein, who lived in Bern and Zurich for several years, reinterpreted it in 1915 in the **general theory of relativity**. For him gravitation is a curving of space and time by mass. For everyday life and for the orbits of satellites, Newton's description is usually quite enough.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which one kilogram is attracted at a place, measured in N/kg.
An imaginary line that shows in which direction the force acts in the field.
A surface of equal gravity that roughly corresponds to mean sea level.
A measure of how much energy one kilogram has at a particular place in the field.

gewusst: On the Moon you weigh only about a sixth as much as on Earth, because its gravitational field is much weaker.
You yourself also have a tiny gravitational field, but it is far too weak to feel.
On Earth there are measurable differences in gravity from place to place, which geologists use to search for raw materials.

teile.einleitung: Thin-film interference is the reason why soap bubbles and oil patches shimmer in all the colours of the rainbow. Light is reflected at the front and at the back of a very thin layer, and the two light waves overlap. Depending on the thickness of the layer, certain colours are reinforced and others cancelled out.
wichtigste: Light is reflected at the front and back of a thin layer and interferes.
Depending on the thickness of the layer, different colours are reinforced, which is why soap bubbles shimmer.
When light is reflected from an optically denser medium, there is a phase shift of half a wavelength.
A soap film that is much thinner than the wavelength looks black.
Anti-reflective coatings on glasses use destructive interference.
An anti-reflective coating with a refractive index of 1.38 must be about 100 nanometres thick for 550 nanometres.
A curved lens on a glass plate produces Newton's rings.
The shimmering blue of some morpho butterflies comes from interference in fine scale structures.

abschnitte.text: The skin of a soap bubble is only a few hundred **nanometres** thick, much thinner than a hair. Part of the light is reflected at its outer surface, another part at its inner surface. The two light waves travel paths of different length and overlap. Because the skin is of different thickness in different places and the water flows, the colours keep moving.

White light contains all colours with different **wavelengths**. At a particular thickness of the layer, crest meets crest for one colour, and that colour is reinforced. Other colours, on the other hand, partly cancel out. The **phase shift** also matters: when light is reflected from an optically denser material, the wave shifts by half a wavelength.

Shortly before a soap bubble bursts, its skin often turns black at the top. There the layer is much thinner than the wavelength of light. Because of the phase shift at the outer surface, the two reflected waves then cancel out for all colours. A soap film with a refractive index of 1.33 and a thickness of 100 nanometres, on the other hand, reinforces green light of 532 nanometres.

Spectacle lenses and camera lenses carry a very thin **anti-reflective coating**. Its thickness is chosen so that the light reflected at its top and bottom surfaces cancels out. With a coating of refractive index 1.38 and green light of 550 nanometres, this needs a thickness of about 100 nanometres, a quarter of the wavelength in the material. As a result the lenses reflect less and let more light through; they often shimmer slightly violet or greenish.

A thin film of oil on a wet road shimmers in colours because light interferes at its top and bottom surfaces. Some **morpho butterflies** from Central and South America glow blue even though their wings contain hardly any blue pigment. Their scales have fine layered structures in which light interferes. If you place a slightly curved lens on a glass plate, **Newton's rings** appear, named after Isaac Newton, who studied them closely.

begriffe.erklaerung: One millionth of a millimetre.
Sudden shift of a wave when it is reflected.
Number that shows how strongly a material slows light down.
Thin coating that reduces unwanted reflections.

gewusst: The colours of a morpho butterfly are called structural colours, because they come from tiny structures and not from pigments.
From the colour of a soap film you can estimate its thickness to within a few nanometres.
The shimmer of mother-of-pearl in seashells also comes from light interfering in many thin layers.

teile.einleitung: Electrostatic induction is a shift of charge in a metal that happens when you bring an electrically charged object close to it. You do not even have to touch the metal. Electrostatic induction explains why charged objects also attract uncharged pieces of metal.
wichtigste: Electrostatic induction is the shift of charge in a conductor caused by an external electric field.
If you bring a negatively charged rod close, positive charge forms on the side of the metal facing it.
The total charge of an insulated conductor stays zero.
An uncharged metal ball is attracted because the opposite charge is closer to the rod.
By briefly earthing a conductor, you can charge it permanently by induction.
In insulators the similar process is called dielectric polarisation.
An electroscope deflects as soon as you just bring a charged rod near it.
The Wimshurst machine produces high voltages through repeated induction.

abschnitte.text: Metals contain many freely moving **electrons**. If you bring a negatively charged rod close, these electrons are repelled and move to the far side. The near side is left with a lack of electrons, so it becomes positive. Overall the conductor stays neutral; the charges have only been shifted.

The positive side of the metal is closer to the negatively charged rod than the negative side. Because electrical forces get weaker with distance, the attraction is greater than the repulsion. That is why an uncharged metal ball or a light ball of aluminium foil is attracted by the rod. With scraps of paper or hair, which are not conductors, the charges shift only within the molecules; this is called **dielectric polarisation**.

You can charge a conductor permanently by induction. To do this, bring a negatively charged rod close and briefly connect the ball to **earth**, for example with your finger. The repelled electrons flow away. If you remove the earth connection and only then take the rod away, the ball stays positively charged.

An **electroscope** is a simple measuring device with a metal rod and a light, movable pointer or two thin leaves. If you bring a charged rod near it without touching it, charges are shifted into the pointer. Pointer and rod then carry the same charge and repel each other, so the electroscope deflects. When you take the rod away, the pointer drops back again.

The **Wimshurst machine** from the late 19th century has two discs with metal plates that rotate in opposite directions. Through repeated induction it produces such high voltages that sparks jump across. Induction also explains the **Faraday cage**: in a closed metal shell the charges shift so that there is no electric field inside. That is why you are fairly well protected in a thunderstorm inside a car or a metal cable car cabin.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material in which electric charges can move freely, for example metal.
Conducting connection to the ground through which charge can flow away.
Device that makes electric charge visible.
Metal shell with no electric field inside.

gewusst: The German word for this effect, Influenz, comes from the Latin influere, which means to flow in.
A balloon that has been rubbed on your hair sticks to the wall because of polarisation.
An aeroplane also acts like a Faraday cage, which is why passengers are protected if lightning strikes.

teile.einleitung: Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure that a liquid at rest exerts because of its own weight. The deeper you dive, the more water there is above you and the greater the pressure becomes. You can already feel this in your ears when diving in a swimming pool.
wichtigste: Hydrostatic pressure is calculated with p = ρ · g · h.
It depends only on the density of the liquid, gravitational acceleration and depth.
At the surface of a liquid at rest, the hydrostatic pressure is zero.
In water the pressure rises by about 1 bar every 10 metres.
At the deepest point of Lake Zurich, 136 metres down, it is around 13 bar.
In the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the oceans, it is around 1100 bar.
The shape of the container makes no difference to the pressure at the bottom.

abschnitte.text: Water is heavy: one cubic metre weighs about 1000 kilograms. That is why every layer of water presses on everything beneath it. This pressure in a liquid at rest is called **hydrostatic pressure**. It acts equally in all directions, so downwards, sideways and also upwards.

It is calculated with p = ρ · g · h. Here ρ (pronounced rho) is the **density** of the liquid, g is gravitational acceleration and h is the depth. At a water depth of 3 metres this gives around 29.4 kilopascals. At a sea depth of 20 metres it is around 201 kilopascals, or about 2 bar, because salt water is denser.

In fresh water the pressure rises by roughly 1 **bar** every 10 metres. At the deepest point of Lake Zurich, 136 metres below the surface, it is around 13 bar. In the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, about 10,935 metres deep, it is about 1100 bar. In 1960 the Swiss Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh became the first to reach the sea floor there in the submersible Trieste, which had been developed by his father Auguste Piccard.

Because pressure increases with depth, **dams** are much thicker at the bottom than at the top. The Grande Dixence dam in Valais, at 285 metres, is the tallest gravity dam in the world. At its foot the water presses against the concrete with enormous force. Water towers also use hydrostatic pressure to get water up to the top floors of houses.

Even at a depth of 2 to 3 metres you feel the pressure in your ears, because the water presses on your **eardrum**. Divers equalise the pressure by gently pushing air into their ears. With mercury, which is much denser than water, the pressure is already around 66 kilopascals at a height of just 0.5 metres. That is why mercury used to be used in barometers to measure air pressure with a short column.

The pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the liquid, not on the shape of the container or the amount in it. This surprising fact is called the **hydrostatic paradox**. In the 17th century the Frenchman Blaise Pascal is said to have burst a barrel with a long, thin tube by pouring water into the top of the tube. The unit of pressure, the pascal, is named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on an area, measured in pascals or bar.
How much mass there is in a certain volume, for example 1000 kg per cubic metre for water.
A unit of pressure: 1 bar is roughly the air pressure at sea level.
The unit of pressure: one newton per square metre.
The pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the liquid, not on the shape of the container.

gewusst: In the Challenger Deep the water presses on every square centimetre as hard as more than a tonne of weight.
A snorkel cannot be as long as you like, because even at a depth of one metre the water pressure makes breathing in very difficult.
Deep sea fish have no air-filled cavities that could be crushed, which is why they survive the enormous pressure.

teile.einleitung: Primary colours are colours from which many other colours can be made by mixing, but which cannot themselves be mixed from other colours. Which colours are primary colours depends on whether you are mixing light or paints. In art lessons red, yellow and blue are often named; on a screen they are red, green and blue.
wichtigste: Primary colours cannot be mixed from other colours.
In art lessons red, yellow and blue are often called primary colours.
Screens put together all colours from the light colours red, green and blue.
Colour printers use cyan, magenta and yellow as well as black.
If you mix two primary colours, you get a mixed colour.
In the paintbox green is not a primary colour; you mix it from yellow and blue.
With at least three primary colours you can mix a great many colours.

abschnitte.text: **Primary colours** are the starting colours of a colour system. A great many other colours can be made from them by mixing, but they themselves cannot be mixed from other colours of the system. You need at least three primary colours to get a wide variety of colours. Colours mixed from two primary colours are called **mixed colours**.

In art lessons red, yellow and blue are often considered the primary colours. Yellow and blue make green, yellow and red make orange, red and blue make violet. So green is not a primary colour, but a mixed colour. This division also goes back to the colour wheel of the Swiss artist **Johannes Itten**.

A screen consists of tiny dots that glow red, green and blue, **RGB** for short. When red and green glow together, you see yellow; when all three glow brightly, you see white. This kind of mixing is called **additive colour mixing**, because light is added. With a magnifying glass you can see the small coloured dots on some screens.

A colour printer uses the colours cyan, magenta and yellow as well as black, **CMYK** for short. Printing inks absorb part of the light and reflect only the rest. That is why this is called **subtractive colour mixing**: the more ink you mix, the darker it gets. Black is used as well because the three colours together give only a dirty dark brown, and black is cheaper for text.

In the retina of the eye there are three kinds of **cones**, which are sense cells for colours. They react especially to red, green and blue light. From the mixture of their signals the brain creates all the colours we see. That is why three suitable primary colours are enough to show us a great many colours.

begriffe.erklaerung: A colour mixed from two or more primary colours.
Red, green and blue, the light colours of screens.
Cyan, magenta, yellow and black, the printing colours.
Sense cells in the eye that recognise colours.

gewusst: On a screen yellow is made from red and green light, although in the paintbox red and green rather give you brown.
The K in CMYK stands for key, the key colour black.
Some animals, such as many birds, have four kinds of cones and can even see ultraviolet light.

teile.einleitung: Gravitation, also called gravity, is the force of attraction between all bodies that have mass. It makes a ball thrown up into the air fall down again, keeps the Moon in its orbit around the Earth and the Earth in its orbit around the Sun. Although it is the weakest of the fundamental forces, it shapes the whole universe.
wichtigste: Gravitation is the force with which all masses attract each other.
The greater the masses, the stronger the attraction.
If you double the distance, the force falls to a quarter.
Isaac Newton described gravitation in 1687 in his law of gravitation.
In 1797 and 1798 Henry Cavendish was the first to measure the attraction between two masses in the laboratory.
Gravitation keeps the planets in their orbits around the Sun.
To leave the Earth completely, you need about 11.2 kilometres per second.

abschnitte.text: Everything that has mass attracts everything else: you, your dog, a mountain and the Earth. Between small things this **gravitation** is so tiny that you cannot feel it. Only very large masses such as the Earth pull noticeably. That is why a ball thrown up always falls down again and we stand safely on the ground.

The English physicist **Isaac Newton** published his law of gravitation in 1687. It says that the attraction grows with the masses and decreases with the square of the distance. So if you double the distance between two bodies, the force falls to a quarter. Newton realised that the same force makes an apple fall and steers the Moon around the Earth.

Because the attraction between everyday objects is so weak, it was hard to measure for a long time. In 1797 and 1798 the Englishman **Henry Cavendish** succeeded with a sensitive torsion balance. Small lead balls hung from a wire and were pulled a tiny distance by large lead balls. From his measurements it was later even possible to calculate the mass of the Earth.

As early as 1609 and 1619 **Johannes Kepler** described the orbits of the planets in three laws. The third says that the squares of the orbital periods are in the same ratio as the cubes of the semi-major axes, so distant planets take much longer for one lap. Newton was able to explain these laws with gravitation. Geostationary satellites circle above the equator at a height of about 35,800 kilometres and seem to stand still in the sky.

The Moon pulls much more weakly than the Earth; its acceleration due to gravity is only about 1.62 m/s². An astronaut with a mass of 60 kg has a weight of about 97 N there, while on Earth it would be almost 590 N. The Moon in turn pulls on the Earth's oceans and so causes the **tides**, that is ebb and flood. At the seaside you can observe this every day.

Albert Einstein, who worked in Bern for several years, presented his general theory of relativity in 1915. In it, gravitation is a curving of space and time by masses. This theory also predicted **gravitational waves**, which were first measured in 2015. Anyone who wants to fly into space and leave the Earth completely must reach the escape velocity of about 11.2 kilometres per second.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for gravitation, the attraction between masses.
Shows how quickly a falling body keeps getting faster; on Earth about 9.81 m/s².
The minimum speed needed to escape completely from the pull of a body in space.
The regular rise and fall of the sea level, caused mainly by the Moon.
A body in space with gravity so strong that not even light escapes.

gewusst: You also pull on the Earth, but it hardly moves because of its huge mass.
Without air resistance a feather and a hammer fall equally fast, as an astronaut showed on the Moon in 1971.
Near a black hole gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

teile.einleitung: The law of conservation of momentum is one of the most important laws of physics. It says that the total momentum of a system stays the same as long as no external forces act on it. It can be used to explain collisions, rockets and even processes inside atoms.
