wichtigste: Without external forces the total momentum of a system is conserved.
This applies to elastic and to inelastic collisions.
If an object at rest breaks apart in an internal explosion, the total momentum of the fragments afterwards is zero.
In oblique collisions you calculate each direction separately.
According to Noether's theorem, conservation of momentum follows from the translation symmetry of space.
In 1930 Wolfgang Pauli predicted the neutrino, partly to save the conservation of momentum in beta decay.
Rockets fly by the recoil principle, which is based on the conservation of momentum.

abschnitte.text: The **law of conservation of momentum** says: in a closed system the sum of all momenta before and after an event is the same. Closed means that no external forces act. The parts of the system can push, slow down or speed up each other. What one object loses in momentum, the other gains exactly.

In an **elastic collision** objects bounce off without losing kinetic energy, as with snooker balls. In an **inelastic collision** the objects change shape or stick together, and part of the energy turns into heat. But in both cases momentum is conserved. If a trolley of 1 kilogram moving at 4 metres per second hits a stationary trolley of 3 kilograms and then stops, the second one moves on at about 1.3 metres per second.

Because momentum has a direction, movements in the opposite direction count as negative. If a trolley of 2 kilograms moves to the right at 3 metres per second and one of 1 kilogram moves to the left at 2 metres per second, the total momentum is 4 kg·m/s to the right. In an oblique collision on a flat surface you apply the law to each direction separately, so left to right and front to back. This also makes it possible to reconstruct road accidents.

An object at rest has zero momentum. If it bursts, the fragments fly apart in such a way that their total momentum is still zero. That is why you feel **recoil** when firing a gun and why a fire hose pushes backwards. A rocket pushes hot gases out backwards and so gains momentum forwards; this works even in the airless vacuum of space.

In 1918 the German mathematician **Emmy Noether** proved that every conserved quantity is linked to a symmetry of nature. Conservation of momentum follows from the fact that the laws of nature are the same everywhere in space, in other words from the **translation symmetry** of space. When energy and momentum seemed to be missing in radioactive beta decay, Wolfgang Pauli suggested an invisible particle in 1930. This **neutrino** was actually detected in 1956.

begriffe.erklaerung: Group of objects on which no force acts from outside.
Collision in which no kinetic energy is lost.
Movement in the opposite direction when something is thrown away.
Tiny, almost massless particle that hardly reacts with matter.

gewusst: When you step from a rowing boat onto the bank, the boat slides away backwards: that is conservation of momentum.
Wolfgang Pauli worked for many years as a professor at ETH Zurich.
With Newton's cradle, exactly as many balls fly off on the other side as you let go.

teile.einleitung: The hydrostatic paradox is a surprising observation: the pressure of a liquid at the bottom of a container depends only on how high it is filled, not on the shape of the container. A thin, tall tube can therefore press on the bottom just as hard as a wide vat. This sounds contradictory, but physics can explain it exactly.
wichtigste: The pressure on the bottom depends only on the filling height, not on the shape of the container.
The pressure is calculated as density times gravitational acceleration times height.
Simon Stevin described the paradox in the 16th century.
Blaise Pascal is said to have burst a wooden barrel with a little water in a long, thin tube.
With the same base area and filling height, the force on the bottom is the same in all containers.
In containers that are wide at the top, the sloping side walls carry part of the weight of the water.
In containers that are narrow at the top, the force on the bottom is greater than the weight of the liquid.

abschnitte.text: Imagine three containers: one shaped like a cylinder, one wide at the top like a vase and one narrow at the top like a bottle. All have a base area of 20 square centimetres and are filled with water to a height of 30 centimetres. Although they hold different amounts of water, the water in all three presses on the bottom with about 5.9 newtons. This astonishing fact is called the **hydrostatic paradox**.

The **gravitational pressure** in a liquid comes from the weight of the column of water above. It is calculated with the formula pressure equals density times gravitational acceleration times height. The width of the container does not appear in this formula. In a container that is wide at the top, part of the water presses down on the sloping walls, so a scale shows more than the force on the bottom. In a container that is narrow at the top, the walls push back, and the force on the bottom is greater than the weight of the water.

The French scholar Blaise Pascal is said to have put a long, thin tube upright into a closed wooden barrel. When he filled the tube with only a little water, the barrel burst. With a tube 10 metres high and a cross section of 1 square centimetre, an extra force of around 49 kilonewtons acts on a lid measuring 0.5 square metres. That is equal to the weight of about five tonnes.

The Flemish scholar **Simon Stevin** described the hydrostatic paradox as early as the 16th century. He lived in what are now the Netherlands and Belgium and worked on mathematics, mechanics and hydraulic engineering. Stevin also helped make decimal fractions better known in Europe. Later Pascal studied the pressure of liquids more closely, which is why the unit of pressure is called the pascal.

The paradox is important for building **dams**. The water pressure on a dam depends only on the depth of the lake, not on how long or wide the lake is. So a narrow, long reservoir presses just as hard as a wide lake of the same depth. That is why dams like the Grande Dixence in Valais are much thicker at the bottom than at the top, because that is where the pressure is greatest.

begriffe.erklaerung: Statement that at first sounds impossible but is nevertheless true.
The study of liquids at rest and their pressure.
Pressure that a liquid exerts because of its own weight.
Unit of pressure, named after Blaise Pascal.

gewusst: For every 10 metres of water depth the pressure rises by about 1 bar, roughly the whole of the air pressure.
It is not certain whether Pascal really carried out the barrel experiment himself.
For divers too, depth is what matters most: in a narrow mountain lake the water pressure at 10 metres is almost the same as in the open sea.

teile.einleitung: A cable is a line that carries electricity or signals from one place to another. Cables run inside our walls, lie under the roads and even connect continents under the sea. To make them safe, they have a protective plastic sheath.
wichtigste: A power cable consists of metal wires, usually copper, and an insulating sheath.
The individual wires have different coloured coverings so that they can be told apart.
The protective wire for earthing is always green and yellow.
Inside, a cable often consists of many thin wires so that it is flexible.
A cable reel must be fully unwound before you plug in a powerful device.
In towns many power cables lie underground; across the country there are often high-voltage lines on pylons.
Besides power cables there are data cables, for example fibre optic cables for the internet.

abschnitte.text: Inside a power cable are metal **conductors**, usually made of copper because it conducts electricity very well. Each conductor is surrounded by a plastic covering, the **insulation**. It stops current getting out or two wires touching each other. Around everything there is also an outer sheath that protects the cable from damage. Flexible cables contain many fine wires called strands, whereas rigid cables in house walls often have a single thick wire.

So that electricians do not mix anything up, the wires are marked in colours. The **earth wire** is green and yellow, and the neutral wire is blue. The wires that carry the voltage are usually brown, black or grey. If there is a fault, the earth wire carries the current away safely so that nobody gets an electric shock.

You should not put cables under a carpet, because they can be damaged there and get hot without anyone noticing. A **cable reel** must be fully unwound before you plug in a powerful device such as a fan heater. Otherwise the wound-up cable can heat up strongly and even melt. Damaged cables with cracks in the sheath should be replaced straight away. And you never pull on a cable to take a plug out.

In towns and villages most power cables lie under the ground as **underground cables**. Over long distances electricity is often carried by **high-voltage lines** that hang high up on large pylons. These overhead lines are cheaper than underground cables and easier to repair. In Switzerland such lines also cross the Alps to exchange electricity between north and south.

Not every cable carries electricity to run devices. A **fibre optic cable** carries light signals and brings fast internet into the home. Huge submarine cables lie on the sea floor and connect Europe with America and Asia. The first telegraph cable across the Atlantic was laid as early as 1858.

With a **charging cable** you charge your mobile phone, and with an extension cable you can reach a socket further away. A multi-socket adapter shares the power between several devices but must not be overloaded. Modern charging cables such as USB-C can carry power and data at the same time. Headphones, televisions and computers often need their own cables for sound and picture.

begriffe.erklaerung: Material through which current can flow well, for example copper.
Protective plastic covering that does not let current through.
Green and yellow wire that safely carries current into the ground if there is a fault.
Bundle of many thin wires that makes a cable flexible.

gewusst: A single fibre optic cable can carry so much data that millions of people could watch videos at the same time.
More than 95 per cent of internet traffic between continents runs through submarine cables and not via satellites.
A cable reel that is still wound up can heat up so much that the plastic melts.

teile.einleitung: The ideal gas is a simplified model that physicists use to describe how gases behave. The gas particles are imagined as tiny points that whizz around, collide and otherwise do not affect each other. Surprisingly many real gases such as air or helium behave almost exactly like this.
wichtigste: In the model the particles take up no volume of their own and do not attract each other.
Pressure, volume, amount of substance and temperature are linked by the equation p times V equals n times R times T.
The universal gas constant R is about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin.
Real gases behave most like an ideal gas at high temperature and low pressure.
At room temperature helium comes particularly close to an ideal gas.
For an ideal gas the compressibility factor is exactly 1.
An ideal gas never becomes liquid, but a real gas does.
The van der Waals equation describes real gases more accurately.

abschnitte.text: A gas consists of unimaginably many particles moving quickly and randomly. For an **ideal gas** you assume that these particles take up no space themselves and do not attract each other. They just bump into each other elastically now and then, like perfect snooker balls. **Gas pressure** arises because the particles keep hitting the walls of the container.

For an ideal gas the **ideal gas law** applies: pressure times volume equals amount of substance times gas constant times temperature. The temperature must be given in kelvin, which starts at absolute zero at minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. The gas constant R is about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin. One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and normal air pressure.

In the 17th century Robert Boyle and Edme Mariotte found that at the same temperature the volume halves when you double the pressure. Around 1800 Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac studied how gases expand when heated. These laws were later combined into the ideal gas law. In 1910 the Dutchman Johannes Diderik van der Waals received the Nobel Prize for his equation for **real gases**.

Real gas particles have a small **volume of their own** and attract each other weakly. At high temperature and low pressure this hardly matters, and the gas behaves almost ideally. Helium is a good example, because its atoms are small and hardly attract each other. If you cool a real gas strongly and compress it, it becomes liquid, which never happens with an ideal gas.

A bike tyre gets warm when you pump it up, and a balloon shrinks when you put it in the fridge. On a plane, sealed crisp packets puff up because the cabin pressure is lower than on the ground. In air at a pressure of 100 kilopascals, oxygen makes up about 21 per cent, so its **partial pressure** is about 21 kilopascals. Weather balloons and diving cylinders are also calculated with the gas law.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit for a very large number of particles, about 602 sextillion of them.
Temperature unit that starts at 0 at absolute zero.
The share of a single gas in the total pressure of a gas mixture.
Actual gas whose particles take up space and attract each other.

gewusst: If you close an empty plastic bottle at the top of a high Swiss pass, it gets squashed by the higher air pressure down in the valley.
There are more gas particles flying around in one litre of air than there are grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth.
No gas is truly ideal; the model is a useful simplification.

teile.einleitung: Joule heating is the heat produced when electric current flows through a conductor. It makes a toaster glow and a kettle get hot. It is named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule.
wichtigste: Joule heating happens because electrons collide with the building blocks of the metal lattice.
The heating power is calculated as current squared times resistance.
If the current doubles, the heating power becomes four times as large.
If 2 A flow through 5 Ω for one minute, 1200 J of heat are produced.
In a toaster, Joule heating is exactly what it is useful for.
In a light bulb only the thin wire glows, because it has a much greater resistance than the leads.
If you shorten a heating wire at a fixed voltage, its heating power increases.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a wire, many **electrons** move through the metal. They keep colliding with the atoms of the **metal lattice** and give off energy. As a result the atoms vibrate more strongly and the wire gets warm. In this way electrical energy is turned into heat.

James Prescott Joule was an English brewery owner and scientist from the area around Manchester. Around 1841 he found out how the heat produced depends on current and resistance. He also showed that heat and work are two forms of the same **energy**. In his honour, the unit of energy is now called the **joule**.

The heating power is P = I² · R, in other words current times current times **resistance**. At a fixed voltage P = U² : R also applies, so a smaller resistance then gives more heat. An immersion heater of 46 ohms at 230 volts therefore has 1150 watts and gives off 345 kilojoules in 5 minutes. A 100 ohm resistor weighing 2 grams, through which 0.1 amperes flow for 10 seconds, warms up by about 6.3 kelvin if it gives off no heat.

In many devices, heat is exactly what you want. **Toasters**, hairdryers, irons, kettles and electric heaters all work with heating wires or heating coils. In a light bulb the thin tungsten wire gets so hot that it shines brightly. The **fuse** also uses the effect, because its wire melts if the current is too high and breaks the circuit.

Joule heating is often a **loss**, for example in power lines, chargers or computer chips. That is why electricity is carried over long distances at high voltage, because at high voltage less current is needed and less heat is produced. Computers and mobile phones need fans or heat sinks so that the chips do not overheat. Overloaded cables can get so hot that a fire starts, so you should not plug too many devices into one multi-socket adapter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shows how strongly a material holds back current, measured in ohms.
Unit of energy and heat.
Energy per second, measured in watts.
Safety part with a thin wire that melts if there is too much current.

gewusst: Superconductors have no electrical resistance, so no Joule heating at all happens in them.
An old light bulb turns only about 5 per cent of the energy into light; the rest becomes heat.
In many cars the rear window is defrosted with thin heating wires that work on the same principle.

teile.einleitung: An isobaric process is one in which a gas changes while its pressure stays the same. The Greek “isos” means equal and “baros” means weight. If a gas is heated at constant pressure, it expands and does work as it does so.
wichtigste: In an isobaric process the pressure stays constant.
On a p-V diagram it appears as a horizontal line.
For an ideal gas the volume grows in the same proportion as the absolute temperature.
The heat supplied equals the change in enthalpy.
For an ideal gas the difference between the molar heat capacities Cp minus Cv equals the gas constant R.
One mole of ideal gas does about 83 J of work when heated by 10 K.
With a monatomic ideal gas, 40 per cent of the heat is given off as work.

abschnitte.text: A gas is described by the **state variables** pressure, volume and temperature. In an isobaric change the pressure stays the same while volume and temperature change. Imagine a cylinder closed at the top by a piston that moves easily. If you heat the gas inside, it pushes the piston upwards, but the pressure always stays the same.

Around 1802 the French researcher Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac showed that gases expand evenly at constant pressure. For an **ideal gas**, the volume divided by the absolute temperature in kelvin is constant. So if a gas is heated from 300 K to 450 K, its volume grows by half. On a **p-V diagram** this process is drawn as a horizontal line.

When the gas expands, it does **expansion work**, which is calculated as pressure times change in volume. 2 litres of gas at 150 kilopascals, heated from 300 K to 450 K, grow to 3 litres and do 150 joules of work. The heat supplied has to both warm the gas and provide this work. That is why at constant pressure it equals the change in **enthalpy**.

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is called Cp, and the one at constant volume Cv. Cp is larger because part of the heat is lost as work; for an ideal gas it is larger by exactly the **gas constant** R of about 8.31 J per mole and kelvin. A monatomic ideal gas has a Cp of about 20.8 J/(mol·K), so 1 mole needs about 208 J of heat for 10 K. Of this, about 83 J, or 40 per cent, is given off as work.

Most processes in the open air are roughly isobaric, because the **air pressure** stays almost the same. A hot air balloon fills with warm air, which expands and therefore becomes lighter. When cooking in an open pan, the pressure is also that of the surroundings. Chemists, too, usually measure heats of reaction at constant pressure, which is why enthalpy is so important to them.

Isobaric steps occur in many machines. In the **Brayton cycle** of a gas turbine, such as the ones that work in aircraft engines, heat is supplied at constant pressure. In the idealised model of a diesel engine the combustion is also isobaric. Besides the isobaric process there are isochoric, isothermal and adiabatic processes.

begriffe.erklaerung: At constant pressure.
Simplified model of a gas that is easy to calculate with.
Energy quantity whose change equals the heat at constant pressure.
Temperature unit that starts at absolute zero. 0 °C is about 273 K.

gewusst: On weather maps, lines of equal air pressure are also called isobars.
In 1804 Gay-Lussac rose to a height of over 7000 metres in a gas balloon to take air samples.

teile.einleitung: A hypothesis is a reasoned guess that can be checked with observations or experiments. Researchers put forward hypotheses to answer a question or explain something. Only when a hypothesis passes many tests does it become established knowledge.
wichtigste: Hypothesis is the technical word for a scientific guess.
A good hypothesis must be testable with an experiment or an observation.
The word comes from Greek and means “supposition” or “assumption”.
A hypothesis can turn out to be right or wrong.
Even a disproved hypothesis moves research forward.
Well-tested hypotheses can become part of a theory.

abschnitte.text: A **hypothesis** is a guess based on knowledge and observations. It is more than just guessing, because you can give reasons why you put it forward. It is often phrased as an if-then sentence. For example: if a plant gets no light, then it grows less well. This statement can be tested.

Research usually starts with a **question**, for example: why do leaves fall in autumn? Then you put forward a hypothesis. With an **experiment** or careful observations you test whether the guess is right. Then you analyse the results and draw conclusions. This often leads to new questions and new hypotheses.

You can test a hypothesis yourself. Your hypothesis is: cress seeds do not sprout without water. Put seeds on two plates with cotton wool and moisten only one of them. Everything else stays the same, so it is a fair **experiment**. After a few days you will see whether your hypothesis was confirmed or disproved.

In the 20th century the philosopher **Karl Popper** stressed that it must be possible to disprove a scientific hypothesis. This property is called **falsifiability**. The statement “Tomorrow it will rain or it will not rain” is always true, but it tells you nothing. A good hypothesis, on the other hand, makes a clear prediction that could also fail. If an experiment disproves the hypothesis, you have still learnt something important.

If a hypothesis is confirmed again and again by many researchers, it gains trust. Several well-tested hypotheses can together form a **theory** that explains many observations. One example is Copernicus's idea that the Earth goes round the Sun. At first it was disputed; today it is confirmed by countless measurements. But in science everything stays open to new findings.

begriffe.erklaerung: Reasoned guess that can be checked.
Planned test used to check a guess.
Well-tested explanation for many observations.
The property of a statement that it could be disproved by a test.

gewusst: In everyday life “theory” often means a mere guess, but in science a theory is very well supported.
Detectives also work with hypotheses when they think about who the culprit might be and then check it.

teile.einleitung: Gravitational waves are tiny ripples in space and time that arise when very heavy bodies in space such as black holes circle each other and merge. Albert Einstein predicted them more than 100 years ago. Only in 2015 did scientists succeed in measuring them directly, one of the greatest discoveries of modern physics.
wichtigste: Gravitational waves were predicted in theory by Albert Einstein.
They travel at the speed of light.
A gravitational wave stretches and squeezes space across its direction of travel.
In 2015 they were detected directly for the first time, caused by the merging of two black holes.
Detectors such as LIGO measure them with laser interferometers that record tiny changes in length.
Even before that, the shrinking orbit of a double pulsar provided indirect proof.
With LISA, ESA is planning a gravitational wave observatory in space.

abschnitte.text: According to Einstein's **general theory of relativity**, heavy masses curve space, rather as a ball makes a dent in a stretched sheet. When very heavy bodies move violently, ripples arise in this space: **gravitational waves**. They travel through space at the speed of light. As they do so, they alternately stretch and squeeze space across their direction of travel.

**Albert Einstein**, who had worked for several years at the patent office in Bern, predicted gravitational waves in 1916. But he believed they were far too weak ever to be measured. In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a **double pulsar**, that is two neutron stars circling each other. Their orbit shrank exactly as the loss of energy through gravitational waves requires, and for this they received the Nobel Prize in 1993.

A **laser interferometer** such as LIGO in the USA has two tubes kilometres long, set at right angles to each other. A laser beam is split, runs through both arms and is brought together again. When a gravitational wave passes through, one arm becomes a tiny bit longer and the other shorter. This change is much smaller than an atomic nucleus, which is why the devices are built to be extremely sensitive.

On 14 September 2015 both LIGO detectors picked up a signal that came from two merging **black holes**. The event was about 1.3 billion light years away. The signal had the typical shape of a **chirp**, in which frequency and strength rise rapidly just before the merger. In 2017 Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this.

Today LIGO, the European detector Virgo in Italy and other facilities regularly measure gravitational waves. In 2017 the merger of two neutron stars was observed for the first time with both gravitational waves and light. ESA is planning the space observatory **LISA**, with three satellites flying millions of kilometres apart. Researchers at ETH Zurich are also working on this project.

begriffe.erklaerung: Einstein's theory that explains gravity as a curving of space and time.
A body in space with gravity so strong that not even light can escape.
A measuring device that overlays light waves to detect tiny differences in length.
A signal that gets faster and higher and higher, like a short chirp.
The extremely dense remains of a large star that has exploded.

gewusst: If you turn the first measured signal into a sound, it sounds like a short chirp.
The gravitational wave of 2015 had been travelling for over a billion years before it reached the Earth.
The arms of the LIGO detectors are each 4 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: In physics, momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity. It describes how much “oomph” there is in a movement. Momentum is a conserved quantity: in a closed system it is never lost.
wichtigste: Momentum is mass times velocity, as a formula p = m · v.
Its unit is kilograms times metres per second.
Momentum has a direction, namely the direction of motion.
In a closed system the total momentum always stays the same.
In collisions momentum is transferred from one object to another.
Rockets fly thanks to recoil, which is explained by the conservation of momentum.
At the same speed, a heavy lorry has much more momentum than a bike.

abschnitte.text: A rolling lorry is much harder to stop than a football, even if both are moving at the same speed. This is because of **momentum**, which is calculated from mass and velocity. The formula is p = m · v. A bike with its rider, 80 kg together, travelling at 5 m/s, has a momentum of 400 kg·m/s.

Momentum is a **directed quantity**, in other words a vector. It always points in the direction in which the object is moving. Two cars of equal weight driving towards each other at the same speed have a total momentum of zero. That is why you always have to pay attention to direction in calculations.

The **law of conservation of momentum** is one of the most important laws of physics. It says that the total momentum in a closed system stays the same, whatever happens inside it. If in snooker a ball hits a stationary ball straight on, it can stop while the other rolls on at almost the same speed. The momentum has simply been passed on.

If you stand on a skateboard and throw a heavy ball forwards, you roll backwards yourself. This is called **recoil**. Rockets use exactly this principle: they push out hot gases backwards at high speed and are driven forwards as a result. That is how propulsion works even in the airless vacuum of space.

To change an object's momentum you need a force acting over a certain time. The longer this time, the smaller the force needed. That is why **airbags**, seat belts, cycle helmets and gym mats make the braking time longer and impacts gentler. When you catch a ball, too, you let your hands give a little so that it hurts less.

As early as the 17th century the French philosopher René Descartes spoke of a “quantity of motion” that is conserved. **Isaac Newton** put momentum at the centre of his laws of motion in 1687. Today we know that light also has momentum. The idea of solar sails for space probes is based on this.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mass times velocity, the force behind a movement.
Quantity that always stays the same in a closed system.
Quantity with size and direction, often drawn as an arrow.
Movement in the opposite direction when you push something away from yourself.

gewusst: With Newton's cradle and its hanging steel balls, exactly as many balls fly off at the other end as you let go on one side.
A squid swims by recoil, pushing water forcefully out of its body.
A rifle also produces recoil when it is fired, which you feel in your shoulder.

teile.einleitung: Embodied energy, called grey energy in German, is the energy you cannot see in a product: it was used for making, transporting, storing, selling and disposing of it. A smartphone, for example, has already cost a lot of energy before you switch it on for the first time. Anyone who saves embodied energy protects the climate and the environment.
wichtigste: Embodied energy lies in the making, transporting and disposing of a product.
You do not see it on your own electricity bill, because it was used before you bought the product.
A smartphone usually needs most of its energy when it is being made.
Strawberries flown in during winter contain especially large amounts of embodied energy.
Per kilogram of goods, the aeroplane usually causes the most embodied energy.
Cement needs a particularly large amount of energy to make.
Repairing and recycling save a lot of embodied energy.

abschnitte.text: **Embodied energy** is the name for all the energy needed for a product to reach us and later to be disposed of again. This includes mining the raw materials, the factory, packaging, transport, storage, sale and disposal. In German it is called grey energy because it is hidden and you cannot see it directly. It does not appear on your own electricity bill, because it was used before you bought the product.

With a **smartphone**, most of the energy over its whole lifetime is usually used when it is made. Chips, screen and battery need rare raw materials and very complex factories. Charging it at home, by comparison, uses little electricity. Anyone who uses a device for longer or has it **repaired** therefore saves a lot of embodied energy, because no new one has to be made.

Strawberries that come by **aeroplane** from faraway countries in winter contain especially large amounts of embodied energy. Per kilogram of goods, the aeroplane needs much more energy than a ship, a train or a lorry. Vegetables from heated greenhouses can also contain a lot of embodied energy. Seasonal and regional food is therefore often the better choice.

In building, a great deal of embodied energy lies in the materials. For **cement**, limestone is burned in large kilns at over 1400 degrees, which needs an enormous amount of energy. Steel, glass and aluminium are also energy-intensive. That is why it can be more climate-friendly to renovate an old house than to demolish it and build a new one. Wood from Swiss forests, on the other hand, needs comparatively little energy.

In **recycling**, new materials are made from old ones. Melting down aluminium from drinks cans again needs only about 5 per cent of the energy needed for new aluminium from ore. In Switzerland glass, paper and PET can also easily be returned at collection points. But even better than recycling is using things for a long time and passing them on.

Switzerland imports many goods, which is why a large part of the embodied energy of what we consume is used abroad. You can make a big difference: wearing clothes and using appliances for longer, having things repaired or buying second-hand. When shopping, seasonal calendars help you choose fruit and vegetables from the region. Sharing, borrowing and swapping also save embodied energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Hidden energy for making, transporting and disposing of a product.
Reusing used materials.
A natural material such as ore, wood or oil from which products are made.
Harvested at the right time of year.

gewusst: A new smartphone has often already used more energy than you need for charging it over many years.
A recycled aluminium can may be back on the shelf as a new can after just a few weeks.
Cement production is one of the largest sources of CO2 in the world.

teile.einleitung: A kaleidoscope is a tube in which mirrors and coloured pieces create beautiful star-shaped patterns. Every turn makes a new picture that almost never comes back. It was invented about 200 years ago in Scotland.
wichtigste: A kaleidoscope contains mirrors and coloured pieces.
When you look in, you see colourful, regular patterns like a star.
If you turn the kaleidoscope, the pattern changes.
You almost never see the same pattern again.
The word kaleidoscope means roughly “seeing beautiful shapes”.
The kaleidoscope was invented about 200 years ago by David Brewster.
When you look into it, it is best to hold it up to the light.

abschnitte.text: A kaleidoscope is an **optical toy** shaped like a tube with a peephole at one end. Inside there are two or three long **mirrors** set at an angle to each other. At the other end there is a chamber with small pieces of coloured glass, beads or bits of plastic. If you hold the tube up to the light and look in, a colourful pattern appears.

The mirrors reflect the image of the coloured pieces back and forth again and again. As a result a small piece is repeated many times and arranged all the way round. If two mirrors are at an angle of 60 degrees, you see the image six times; at 45 degrees, eight times. This creates a **symmetrical** pattern that looks like a star or a snowflake.

When you turn the kaleidoscope, the pieces tumble about and form a new pattern. Because they lie a little differently each time, you almost never see exactly the same picture again. There are so many possible arrangements that you could keep turning it all your life. In a **teleidoscope** there are no pieces; instead you see your surroundings through a lens as a pattern.

The Scottish physicist **David Brewster** invented the kaleidoscope in 1816 during experiments with light and mirrors. He patented it in 1817, but the toy was copied so quickly that he hardly earned anything from it. Within a few months hundreds of thousands of kaleidoscopes were sold. Brewster made up the name from the Greek words **kalos** for beautiful, eidos for shape and skopein for looking at.

Today there are kaleidoscopes as simple children's toys made of cardboard and as precious works of art made of brass and glass. Their patterns serve designers as models for fabrics, wallpapers and tiles. Kaleidoscope pictures can also be created on a computer. In a figurative sense people say “a kaleidoscope of impressions” when they mean many colourful, changing experiences.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mirror throws back the light and shows an image.
Regularity in which parts of a picture repeat exactly.
Legal right that reserves an invention for its inventor for a certain time.

gewusst: You can build a simple kaleidoscope yourself with three strips of mirror, a cardboard tube and a few coloured beads.
David Brewster also researched how light is refracted in crystals.

teile.einleitung: An integrated circuit, often just called a chip, is a tiny electronic circuit on a small wafer of silicon. Billions of components sit on just a few square centimetres. Chips are found in mobile phones, computers, cars and even washing machines.
wichtigste: An integrated circuit combines many components on a single piece of semiconductor.
Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit in 1958 and received the Nobel Prize in 2000.
The Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented the planar process for mass production in 1959.
The structures are transferred onto the wafer with light by photolithography.
EUV lithography works with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres.
Chips are made in clean rooms, because even tiny dust particles would destroy them.
The Intel 4004 of 1971 was the first commercially available single-chip processor.
A single chip piece sawn out of the wafer is called a die.

abschnitte.text: An **integrated circuit** (IC for short) contains transistors, resistors and conducting tracks on a single small piece. In the past, circuits were built from separate components that were soldered together with wires. In a chip, everything is built into one piece of **semiconductor**, usually silicon. This makes the circuit tiny, fast, cheap and reliable.

In 1958 the engineer **Jack Kilby** built the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in the USA, and in 2000 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it. Soon afterwards Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor developed a chip made of silicon. This was made possible by the **planar process**, which the Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented in 1959. It allowed chips to be made flat and in large numbers.

The starting point is a thin, round silicon disc, the **wafer**. With **photolithography** the circuit pattern is transferred with light through a mask onto a light-sensitive layer, as with a photo. For the finest structures, extreme ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres is used. Then the wafer is sawn into many separate pieces called dies, and each goes into a protective casing.

Because the structures are a thousand times thinner than a hair, even a single grain of dust would destroy a conducting track. That is why chips are made in **clean rooms**, where the air is filtered all the time. The workers wear full-body suits, hoods and masks. The air there is much cleaner than in an operating theatre.

In 1971 Intel brought out the **4004**, the first commercially available microprocessor on a single chip, with about 2300 transistors. Today's processors contain many billions of transistors. As early as 1965 Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double regularly. This prediction is called **Moore's law** and held up astonishingly well for decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny electronic switch that can turn current on and off.
Material such as silicon that conducts current or not, depending on conditions.
Thin silicon disc on which many chips are made at the same time.
Process that transfers circuit patterns onto the wafer with light.

gewusst: A modern mobile phone chip contains more transistors than there are people on Earth.
Jean Hoerni, the inventor of the planar process, was born in Geneva in 1924.
Silicon is obtained from quartz sand, one of the most common materials in the Earth's crust.

teile.einleitung: The golden rule of mechanics says: what you save in force, you must add in distance. Whether a lever, a block and tackle or a ramp, no simple machine saves work. It only shares the work out differently between force and distance.
wichtigste: What you save in force, you must add in distance.
In a simple machine without friction, the work stays the same.
Work is force times distance and is measured in joules.
One joule is one newton times one metre.
Behind the golden rule lies the law of conservation of energy.
Friction means that in reality you have to put in more work.

abschnitte.text: The **golden rule of mechanics** applies to all simple machines such as levers, pulleys, blocks and tackles and inclined planes. It says that with these aids you can save force, but in return you have to cover a longer distance. The product of force and distance, the **work**, stays the same without friction. So you can lift a heavy load with little force, but you have to pull or push for longer.

Mechanical work is calculated as force times distance. Its unit is the **joule**, named after the Englishman James Prescott Joule. One joule is one newton times one metre. To lift a load of 500 N by 2 metres, you need 1000 joules without friction, whatever aid you use.

A ramp is a good example of the golden rule. If you want to raise a crate weighing 300 N by 1.5 metres, the work is 450 joules. If you push it up an **inclined plane** 6 metres long, you need only 75 N without friction. The distance is four times as long, but the force is four times smaller.

In a **block and tackle** a rope runs over several pulleys. If you use it to lift 400 N by 3 metres and pull with only 100 N, you have to pull 12 metres of rope. The same applies to the lever: the long arm of the lever moves a long way, the short arm only a little. Such blocks and tackles have been used on building sites and sailing ships for centuries.

Behind the golden rule lies the **law of conservation of energy**: energy cannot come from nothing. That is why no machine can give out more work than you put in. In reality, friction always produces some heat, and you have to put in more work. The ratio of useful work to work put in is called **efficiency**.

Even in ancient Greece people knew levers, pulleys and wedges. Archimedes and later Hero of Alexandria described how to move large loads with them. Around 1600 Galileo Galilei clearly recognised that simple machines do not save work. The name golden rule shows how important this principle is for mechanics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force times distance, the amount of energy needed to move or lift something.
The unit of work and energy: one newton times one metre.
An aid such as a lever, pulley or ramp that changes force or direction.
How much of the work put in is really used in the end.
Energy is never lost and never comes from nothing; it is only converted.

gewusst: Mountain roads with many hairpin bends, such as on the Gotthard, are a huge inclined plane that saves force but makes the distance longer.
A perpetual motion machine that runs for ever without a supply of energy is impossible because of the conservation of energy.
A bike in a low gear also uses the golden rule: pedalling is easier, but you have to pedal more often.

teile.einleitung: Terminal velocity is the highest speed a falling body can reach in air or water. It is reached when air resistance brakes just as strongly as gravity pulls. That is why raindrops, skydivers and snowflakes do not keep getting faster.
wichtigste: A falling body reaches terminal velocity when air resistance and weight are equal.
At terminal velocity the acceleration is zero, and the body keeps falling at a steady speed.
A skydiver lying on their stomach falls at about 200 km/h.
Large raindrops fall at most about 30 km/h.
Heavy, compact bodies have a higher terminal velocity than light, bulky ones.
In thin air the terminal velocity is much higher than in dense air.
Small animals such as mice often survive falls unhurt, because their terminal velocity is very low.

abschnitte.text: At the start of a fall, **weight** pulls the body down, and it keeps getting faster. The faster it falls, the more strongly **air resistance** brakes it. This grows roughly with the square of the speed, so at twice the speed it becomes four times as large. At some point the two forces are equal and cancel each other out. From this moment the body no longer accelerates and falls at a constant speed, the **terminal velocity**.

What matters are the mass, the shape and the area the body presents to the air. An iron ball and a wooden ball of the same size have the same air resistance, but the iron ball is much heavier. That is why the iron ball reaches a higher terminal velocity. A flat feather or a sheet of paper, on the other hand, falls very slowly. The **density of the air** also plays a part: in thin air high up, the resistance is smaller.

A skydiver lying on their stomach with arms spread out falls at about 200 km/h. If they dive head first, they present much less area to the air and become much faster. When they open the parachute, the area suddenly becomes huge and the terminal velocity falls to a few metres per second. In this way they can land gently. In Switzerland the Lauterbrunnen valley in the Bernese Oberland is known for BASE jumpers who jump from rock faces.

In 2012 the Austrian **Felix Baumgartner** jumped from a capsule under a balloon at a height of almost 39 kilometres. At this height the air is very thin and hardly brakes at all. That is why he became faster than sound in free fall and reached over 1300 km/h. Further down, where the air becomes denser, air resistance slowed him down strongly again. In the end he landed safely with his parachute.

Large **raindrops** fall at most about 30 km/h, and small drizzle drops much more slowly still. Snowflakes sink gently to the ground because of their large, loose shape. Small animals such as mice or insects have a large surface area in relation to their weight. Their terminal velocity is so low that they often survive a fall from a great height unhurt. Plant seeds such as those of the dandelion also make use of this to fly a long way on the wind.

begriffe.erklaerung: A braking force that arises when a body moves through the air.
The force with which the Earth pulls a body downwards.
How quickly the speed of a body changes.
A layer of air high above the clouds, where the air is very thin.

gewusst: Without air resistance, a raindrop falling from a height of 1000 metres would hit the ground at over 500 km/h.
Wingsuit flyers slow down their fall with a suit that has fabric surfaces between the arms and legs.
In a vacuum there is no terminal velocity; there a feather and a hammer fall equally fast.

teile.einleitung: Seasons are parts of the year in which weather, temperature and the length of the day change in a typical way. Here they are spring, summer, autumn and winter. They happen because the Earth's axis is tilted while the Earth travels round the Sun for a year.
wichtigste: There are seasons because the Earth's axis is tilted.
Here we have spring, summer, autumn and winter.
Astronomical spring begins around 20 March, autumn in September.
When it is summer here, it is winter in Australia.
At the equator there is often a rainy season and a dry season instead of summer and winter.
The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January, not in summer.
A year has 365 days, a leap year 366 days.

abschnitte.text: The Earth travels once round the Sun in a year. Its **axis** is tilted by about 23.4 degrees and always points in the same direction in space. That is why sometimes the northern hemisphere and sometimes the southern hemisphere is tilted more towards the Sun. In summer the Sun is high in our sky, its rays hit the ground steeply and the days are long.

Many people think the Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. That is not true: it is closest at the beginning of January, in the middle of our winter. What matters is the **angle** at which the Sun's rays arrive. When they arrive at a slant, the warmth is spread over a larger area, like the light of a torch held at an angle.

According to the calendar of the stars, **spring** begins around 20 March, when day and night are the same length. Summer begins around 21 June with the longest day, and autumn around 22 or 23 September. Winter begins around 21 December with the shortest day. Weather experts, on the other hand, use **meteorological seasons**, which begin on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December.

In the southern hemisphere the seasons are the other way round: when it is summer here, it is winter in Australia. People there often celebrate Christmas on the beach. In many countries near the **equator** it is warm all year round, and instead they have a rainy season and a dry season. Near the poles the Sun stays in the sky for weeks in summer, while in winter there is the **polar night**.

In spring trees come into leaf and migratory birds return. In summer fruit and grain grow, and in autumn the leaves change colour and fall. In winter animals such as the marmot **hibernate**, while others grow a thick winter coat. For a long time people also arranged their lives around the seasons, for example for sowing and harvesting.

In Switzerland the seasons shape life strongly, especially in the mountains. In early summer farmers take their cows up to the alpine pastures, and in autumn they bring them back down in the **Alpabzug**. In winter there is often snow in the Alps, and many people go skiing or sledging. Customs such as the Sechseläuten in Zurich, where the Böögg is burnt, celebrate the end of winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: Imaginary line through the North and South Poles around which the Earth turns.
Imaginary line around the middle of the Earth.
Time when the Sun does not rise for days near the poles.
Year with 366 days, because 29 February is added.

gewusst: Without a tilted axis there would be practically no seasons on Earth.
Because one orbit of the Earth takes about 365 days and 6 hours, a leap year with 366 days is needed almost every four years.
On Mars each season lasts almost twice as long as on Earth.

teile.einleitung: In an implosion an object is suddenly squashed inwards by pressure from outside. It is the opposite of an explosion, in which something flies apart outwards. Implosions happen when the pressure inside is much lower than outside.
wichtigste: In an implosion an object is pushed inwards by pressure from outside.
The cause is low pressure inside, for example from cooling steam.
A drinks can filled with hot steam gets crushed when you dip it upside down into cold water.
A sealed tank wagon that cools down can be crushed by air pressure.
Old tube televisions could implode when they broke, because their picture tube contained a vacuum.
Submarines cannot dive as deep as they like, because the water pressure could crush the hull.
The lid of a jar of jam filled while hot sits tightly because of the low pressure.

abschnitte.text: In an **implosion** a hollow object suddenly collapses inwards. This happens when the pressure from outside is much greater than the **pressure inside**. Air pressure at sea level is about 1 bar, which equals the weight of around 10 tonnes on every square metre. If there is no counter pressure inside, this force can crush thin metal or glass.

You heat a little water in an empty drinks can until steam forms. The **steam** pushes the air out of the can. Then you dip the can upside down into cold water so that no air can flow back in. The steam condenses in a flash into a few drops, and the air pressure outside crushes the can with a bang.

After being cleaned with hot steam, railway tank wagons can become dangerous. If they are sealed while the steam cools, **low pressure** forms and the air pressure crushes the huge steel tank. A PET bottle rinsed with hot water and sealed straight away also shrinks as it cools. As early as the 17th century Otto von Guericke showed with the Magdeburg hemispheres how enormous air pressure is.

Old televisions had a large glass **picture tube** with almost no air in it. If it broke, glass splinters could fly first inwards and then in all directions. For submarines, at great depth the water presses from outside with tremendous force. That is why they have a maximum diving depth that they must not exceed.

When **preserving**, you fill jars with hot jam and seal them straight away. As they cool, low pressure forms in the jar and the lid is sucked on tightly. This protects the jam from germs for a long time. When you open such a jar you often hear a pop, because air rushes in.

Huge stars can implode too. When their fuel is used up, their core collapses under its own gravity in a fraction of a second. This can create a neutron star or a black hole. The outer layers are flung away in a tremendous **supernova**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sudden inward collapse of an object caused by pressure from outside.
A pressure that is lower than the air pressure of the surroundings.
When steam cools and turns back into liquid water.
The pressure that the air of the Earth's atmosphere exerts on everything.

gewusst: When tower blocks are demolished with explosives, people often call it an implosion, because they are made to collapse inwards cleverly.
Air pressure presses on the palm of your hand with a force equal to about 100 kilograms; we just do not notice because it is pushed back equally hard from inside.
With the Magdeburg hemispheres, even teams of horses could not pull apart the hemispheres once the air had been pumped out.

teile.einleitung: A yo-yo is a toy made of two discs joined by an axle with a string wound around it. If you let it fall, it unrolls and then climbs back up as if by magic. Behind it lies exciting physics of energy and rotation.
wichtigste: The string of a yo-yo is wound around the axle in the middle.
As it unrolls, potential energy turns into kinetic and rotational energy.
A yo-yo falls more slowly than a stone in free fall, because part of the energy goes into the spin.
At the bottom the spin winds the string back up, which is why the yo-yo climbs.
If you throw it down hard, it spins faster at the bottom.
In the trick called the “sleeper”, the yo-yo spins on the spot at the bottom for a long time.
There were already pictures of yo-yo-like toys on vases in ancient Greece.

abschnitte.text: A yo-yo consists of two round **discs** joined in the middle by a narrow **axle**. A string is wound around the axle, and its end is fixed to your finger with a loop. In the past yo-yos were mostly made of wood; today they are often made of plastic or metal. Modern models have a **ball bearing** so that they spin very easily.

When you hold the yo-yo up, it has **potential energy**. As it falls, this is turned into kinetic energy and **rotational energy**, because the yo-yo falls and spins at the same time. Because a large part of the energy goes into the spin, it falls much more slowly than a stone. Much as with a pendulum, potential and kinetic energy keep taking turns.

At the bottom, at the end of the string, the yo-yo keeps spinning very fast. This spin winds the string back up, so the yo-yo climbs upwards. Because some energy is lost through **friction**, it never quite reaches its starting height. That is why you always give a small tug with your hand to supply the missing energy.

In the **sleeper**, the yo-yo spins on the spot at the bottom for a long time, because the string lies only loosely around a ball bearing. Many other tricks build on this one, such as “Walk the Dog”, in which the yo-yo rolls along the floor. If you throw it down hard, it spins faster and sleeps longer. At yo-yo world championships, players from all over the world show difficult tricks.

Vases from **ancient Greece** already show children with yo-yo-like discs. Later the toy was popular in Asia and, in the 18th century, in France too. The name yo-yo probably comes from the **Philippines**. Pedro Flores, an immigrant from the Philippines, opened a yo-yo factory in California in the 1920s and made the toy famous in America.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that an object has because it is high up.
Energy contained in a spinning movement.
Part in the middle around which something turns.
Yo-yo trick in which it spins on the spot at the bottom for a long time.

gewusst: In 1985 astronauts took a yo-yo into space to see how it works in weightlessness.
Without gravity a yo-yo does not fall by itself; you have to throw it away hard.
Good yo-yos with ball bearings can spin on the spot for many minutes.

teile.einleitung: A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot or cold for hours. Many people simply call it a Thermos flask, after a well-known brand. Its secret is two walls with an almost airless space between them.
wichtigste: A vacuum flask keeps drinks warm or cold for a long time.
Another word for a vacuum flask is Thermos flask.
It has two walls, and there is almost no air between them.
The airless space, the vacuum, strongly slows down the transfer of heat.
The lid must be closed tightly, otherwise the heat escapes.
Hot tea does not stay hot for ever, but slowly cools down.
In summer the flask can also keep cold water cool.

abschnitte.text: A vacuum flask is a container that strongly slows down the **exchange of heat** between the drink and the surroundings. It has an inner wall and an outer wall that are joined only at the neck of the flask. The air between them has been almost completely pumped out, creating a **vacuum**. Modern flasks are usually made of stainless steel; older ones had a glass insert.

Heat can travel in three ways: by **conduction**, by the flow of air or liquid, and by radiation. In a vacuum there are hardly any particles that could pass on heat or flow around. To deal with heat radiation, the walls are often mirrored or shiny, so the radiation is reflected back. Because all three paths are slowed down, the flask works equally well for hot and cold drinks.

Around 1892 the Scottish scientist **James Dewar** built a double-walled glass vessel with a vacuum to store very cold, liquid gases. It is still called a **Dewar flask** after him. The German glassblower Reinhold Burger realised that the idea was also useful in everyday life and applied for a patent in 1903. Soon afterwards the flask went on sale under the brand name Thermos.

On a **winter hike** or when skiing, hot tea from a Thermos flask is especially welcome. In summer it keeps water or squash pleasantly cool on a bike ride. Many children take a small vacuum flask to school or on a school trip. If you warm the flask with hot water first, it keeps the drink warm even longer.

A vacuum flask is never perfect; a little heat always escapes through the **lid** and the neck. That is why tea slowly cools down and is often only lukewarm after a day. If the flask is dropped, the vacuum can be damaged, and then it insulates much less well. To clean it, use a brush and rinse it out well so that no smells remain.

begriffe.erklaerung: Space in which there is almost no air and no other particles.
Stop heat or cold from getting out or in quickly.
Passing on of heat from particle to particle, for example through a spoon in hot tea.
Double-walled vessel with a vacuum, named after its inventor James Dewar.

gewusst: In research laboratories, liquid nitrogen at almost minus 200 degrees is stored in large Dewar flasks.
A good vacuum flask can keep tea much warmer for many hours than an ordinary bottle.

teile.einleitung: Glow-worms are not worms but beetles that can glow with their abdomen. They are also called fireflies or, in German, St John's beetles. On warm summer nights in Switzerland you can see their small yellow-green lights in the grass and between bushes.
wichtigste: Glow-worms are beetles and belong to the firefly family.
They glow with a special organ on their abdomen.
Their light is cold; it is produced almost without heat.
In our part of the world glow-worms glow yellow-green.
They glow so that they can find each other in the dark.
The larvae like to eat snails.
A lot of artificial light at night disturbs glow-worms, which is why there are fewer of them.

abschnitte.text: Glow-worms are small, inconspicuous **beetles**, usually about a centimetre long. On their abdomen they have a **light organ** that gives off yellow-green light. In some species the females have no wings and look more like larvae. That is why people used to think they were worms.

The light is produced by a **chemical reaction**: the substance **luciferin** reacts with oxygen, helped by a protein called **luciferase**. In the process almost all the energy is turned into light and hardly any into heat. That is why the light of glow-worms is cold. An old light bulb, on the other hand, turns most of its energy into heat.

Glow-worms are active mainly in June and July, around **St John's Day** on 24 June, which is where the German name St John's beetle comes from. On warm nights the females glow in the grass, and the males fly around looking for them. So the light helps them to find each other. The adult beetles live only a few weeks and hardly eat anything during this time.

Glow-worms spend most of their lives as **larvae**, often for two to three years. The larvae can already glow. They hunt mainly snails, which are often much larger than themselves. They stun the snail with a bite and then digest it from the outside.

abschnitte.titel: Glow-worms in Switzerland and their protection
abschnitte.text: Three species are found in Switzerland; the best known are the **common glow-worm** and the **lesser glow-worm**. They live at the edges of woods, in gardens, hedges and natural meadows. Because many street lamps and lit gardens make the night bright, the animals see each other less well; this is called **light pollution**. Anyone who wants to help glow-worms switches off unnecessary lights at night and leaves wild corners in the garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the body with which an animal can produce light.
The substance that reacts with oxygen in the light organ and produces light.
The ability of living things to produce light themselves.
Too much artificial light at night, which disturbs animals and plants.

gewusst: The light of a glow-worm is one of the most efficient lights there is, much more economical than a light bulb.
Many animals in the deep sea can also produce light themselves, like glow-worms.
In some parts of Asia and America, thousands of fireflies flash at the same time in the same rhythm.

teile.einleitung: In a temperature inversion the air higher up is warmer than down at the ground, exactly the opposite of usual. The Latin word “inversio” means turning upside down. In Switzerland this weather situation brings grey high fog to the Central Plateau in winter and bright sunshine on the mountains.
wichtigste: Normally the air gets colder with height; in an inversion it is warmer above than below.
In winter, inversions often form with an area of high pressure.
On the Swiss Central Plateau an inversion often brings high fog and cold.
On mountains such as the Rigi you can then often see the sun above the sea of fog.
The warm layer acts like a lid, so exhaust fumes stay down below and the air quality is poor.
Together with the high fog, the cold bise often blows across the Central Plateau.
If it is 0 °C in Zurich and 8 °C at a height of 1500 metres, there is an inversion.

abschnitte.text: Normally the temperature drops by about half a degree to one degree for every 100 metres of height. In an inversion, though, there is a layer of air in which it gets warmer going up, the **inversion layer**. Beneath it lies cold, heavy air that cannot rise. That is why this weather situation is also called a **temperature reversal**.

In winter the nights are long, and the ground gives off a lot of heat to the clear sky. The air at the ground cools down strongly and collects in valleys and basins. In an **area of high pressure**, air also sinks from above and warms up as it does so. In this way a warm layer settles over the cold air near the ground, creating a **subsidence inversion**.

abschnitte.titel: Sea of fog over the Central Plateau
abschnitte.text: The Swiss Central Plateau lies like a tub between the Jura and the Alps. In an inversion a thick blanket of **high fog** often forms in the cold, damp air and can stay for days. From above, this cloud cover looks like a **sea of fog**, with the summits sticking out of it like islands. Popular viewpoints include the Rigi, Mount Pilatus, the Weissenstein and the Napf.

The **bise**, a cold, dry northeasterly wind, often blows beneath the blanket of fog. It is funnelled between the Jura and the Alps and blows particularly hard at Lake Geneva. The bise makes the temperatures in the fog feel even colder. While people are freezing in Bern or Zurich, it can be noticeably warmer and sunny at 1500 metres.

The warm layer of air acts like a lid on a pot. Exhaust fumes from traffic, heating and industry cannot escape upwards and collect near the ground. That is why the amount of **fine dust** in the air rises during long inversions. In big cities such as Milan, or London in the past, dense **smog** could form like this.

Inversions do not only happen in winter. On clear summer nights a thin **ground inversion** often forms by the morning and quickly disappears once the sun comes out. There are also inversions high up, which can slow down the rise of thunderclouds, for example. Glider and balloon pilots therefore pay close attention to such layers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Reversal; here: it is warmer above than below.
Region with high air pressure, usually with calm, dry weather.
Fog that does not lie on the ground but hangs over the land like a low blanket of cloud.
Cold, dry wind from the northeast on the Swiss Central Plateau.
Mixture of smoke, exhaust fumes and fog that pollutes the air.

gewusst: In strong inversions it can be more than 10 degrees warmer in the mountains than in the valley below.
The word smog is made up of the English words “smoke” and “fog”.
Hikers and day trippers sometimes call sunny trips above the sea of fog “Nebelflucht”, German for escaping the fog.

teile.einleitung: In physics, momentum is the force behind a movement, how much “oomph” it has. It depends on how heavy an object is and how fast it moves. A slow lorry can therefore have just as much momentum as a fast car.
wichtigste: Momentum is mass times velocity.
Its SI unit is kilograms times metres per second.
Momentum is a vector quantity, so it has a direction.
A ball of 0.16 kilograms moving at 25 metres per second has a momentum of 4 kg·m/s.
A 10 tonne lorry at 1 m/s and a 1 tonne car at 10 m/s have the same momentum.
With the same momentum, the lighter object has more kinetic energy.
Close to the speed of light, momentum is greater than mass times velocity.
Light also has momentum, even though photons have no mass.

abschnitte.text: **Momentum** describes how much motion there is in an object. It is calculated as mass times velocity, and its symbol is usually p. The unit is kilograms times metres per second. A football of 0.16 kilograms flying at 25 metres per second has a momentum of 4 kg·m/s.

Momentum is a **vector quantity**, so it always points in the direction of motion. If a ball of 0.3 kilograms hits a wall head on at 10 metres per second and bounces back just as fast, its momentum is reversed. The change in momentum is then not zero but 6 kg·m/s. That is why a wall feels a ball that bounces off more strongly than one that just drops.

A heavy, slow object can have as much momentum as a light, fast one. A lorry of 10 tonnes moving at 1 metre per second has the same momentum as a car of 1 tonne moving at 10 metres per second. But their **kinetic energy** is different: the faster, lighter car has ten times as much. Energy and momentum are therefore two different quantities.

Isaac Newton realised that a **force** changes the momentum of an object. The shorter the time in which the momentum changes, the greater the force. That is why airbags, cycle helmets and crumple zones protect you: they make the braking time longer and so reduce the force on the body. When landing after a jump you also bend your knees to cushion the impact.

Surprisingly, light also has momentum, even though **photons** have no mass. That is why solar sails in space can be driven by sunlight. If an object moves at almost the speed of light, the simple formula no longer applies. According to Albert Einstein's **theory of relativity**, the momentum is then greater than mass times velocity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mass times velocity, the force behind a movement.
Quantity that has a size and a direction.
Smallest particle of light.
Force times the time it acts; it equals the change in momentum.

gewusst: In German, momentum is called “Impuls”, while the English word impulse means rather the force times its duration.
An ocean ship moving slowly has such enormous momentum that it needs several kilometres to stop.
In 2010 Japan successfully tested a solar sail in space for the first time with the space probe IKAROS.

teile.einleitung: James Watt was a Scottish inventor and engineer who greatly improved the steam engine. His economical engines strongly drove the Industrial Revolution forward. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
wichtigste: James Watt lived from 1736 to 1819 and came from Scotland.
He greatly improved the steam engine.
A separate condenser made his engine much more economical.
With the businessman Matthew Boulton he founded a company making steam engines.
He introduced horsepower to compare engines with horses.
His engines strongly drove the Industrial Revolution forward.
The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

abschnitte.text: James Watt was born in Greenock in **Scotland** in 1736 and died near Birmingham in England in 1819. He first worked as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow. There, around 1763, he was asked to repair a model of a **steam engine** that worked on the principle of Thomas Newcomen. While doing so he noticed how much coal and heat this engine wasted.

In the old engine the cylinder was cooled with cold water at every stroke and then heated up again. In 1765 Watt had the idea of cooling the steam in a **separate condenser**. That way the cylinder stayed hot all the time, and the engine needed much less coal. In 1769 he received a patent for it.

From 1775 Watt built steam engines in Birmingham together with the businessman **Matthew Boulton**. He improved them further so that they could not only pump but also turn wheels. This meant his engines could drive spinning mills, mills and factories. A centrifugal governor made sure the engine ran at an even speed.

To sell his engines, Watt compared them with horses, which drove many pumps at the time. That is how he introduced the unit **horsepower**. In his honour, today's unit of power is called the **watt**, abbreviated W. One horsepower (in its metric form) equals about 735 watts. A motor that does 1200 joules of work in 60 seconds has a power of 20 watts.

Lamps, hairdryers and kettles show how many watts they have. The more watts, the more energy the device uses per second. A 60 watt lamp uses 600 watt hours in 10 hours, or 0.6 **kilowatt hours**. This is exactly the unit that is counted on the electricity bill.

The improved steam engine powered the **Industrial Revolution**, which began in Great Britain. Factories no longer had to stand by rivers with water wheels. Later this led to steam locomotives and steamships, like the ones that still sail on Lake Lucerne or Lake Geneva today. Watt's portrait, together with Matthew Boulton, appeared on a British 50 pound banknote.

begriffe.erklaerung: Machine that produces movement using hot steam.
In a steam engine, a container in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.
How much work or energy is converted per second.
The right to be the only one allowed to use an invention.

gewusst: Watt is said to have had the idea of the separate condenser on a Sunday walk in Glasgow.
One horsepower was originally meant as the work a strong horse can keep up for a long time.
A modern high-speed train has a power of many thousands of kilowatts.

teile.einleitung: Every battery and every other voltage source has an internal resistance, a built-in electrical resistance inside itself. It causes the voltage to drop as soon as a current flows. That is why, for example, a car's headlights dim briefly when the engine is started.
wichtigste: Internal resistance is the resistance inside a voltage source.
With no current, you measure the full open-circuit voltage.
When current flows, the terminal voltage is lower by internal resistance times current.
A 1.5 volt battery with 0.5 ohms internal resistance still delivers 1.3 volts at 0.4 amperes.
Internal resistance limits the short-circuit current.
A source delivers the most power when the load resistance equals the internal resistance.
When a car starts, the voltage drops because of the high starter current, and the headlights dim.

abschnitte.text: A battery supplies current through chemical reactions inside it. The current also has to flow through the materials of the battery itself, and these slow it down a little. This built-in resistance is called **internal resistance**, and it is measured in ohms. So you can picture a battery as an ideal voltage source with a small resistance behind it.

With no device connected, no current flows, and you then measure the **open-circuit voltage**. As soon as current flows, part of the voltage is already lost inside. At the terminals only the **terminal voltage** is left: open-circuit voltage minus internal resistance times current. With a 1.5 volt battery and 0.5 ohms internal resistance, 1.3 volts remain at 0.4 amperes.

You can work out the internal resistance from two measurements. If a source shows 9.0 volts in open circuit and still 8.0 volts at 0.5 amperes, 1 volt has been lost inside. The internal resistance is therefore 1 volt divided by 0.5 amperes, which gives 2 ohms. If you connect two D cells of 1.5 volts and 0.3 ohms each in series to 2.4 ohms, exactly 1 ampere flows, because the voltages and internal resistances add up.

If you connect the terminals directly, only the internal resistance limits the current. A 12 volt car battery with 0.02 ohms internal resistance could then deliver about 600 amperes, enough to make cables glow. The car needs this low internal resistance for the **starter motor**, which draws a lot of current when starting. The voltage drops briefly, and the headlights dim.

A source delivers the greatest possible power to a device when the device's resistance is exactly as large as the internal resistance. This is called **impedance matching**. A source with 6 volts and 3 ohms internal resistance can then deliver at most 3 watts, but half of the energy is turned into heat in the source itself. Flat or cold batteries have a higher internal resistance, which is why mobile phone batteries struggle in winter when you go skiing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Voltage of a source when no current flows.
Voltage at the terminals when current flows.
Unit of electrical resistance.
Direct connection of the terminals with no device in between.

gewusst: A car starter battery has a much smaller internal resistance than a small torch battery.
Battery testers often measure the internal resistance indirectly to see how good a battery still is.
Because a battery heats up through its internal resistance at high current, rechargeable batteries get warm during fast charging.

teile.einleitung: Internal energy is the total energy contained in the tiny particles of an object. It includes the energy of their jiggling movement and the energy of their attraction to each other. When an object gets warmer, its internal energy rises.
wichtigste: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all the particles in a system.
For an ideal gas with a fixed amount of substance it depends only on temperature.
Each degree of freedom of a particle contributes on average one half k times T.
A diatomic molecule such as nitrogen has 5 degrees of freedom at room temperature.
One mole of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 kelvin has about 3.7 kilojoules of internal energy.
After a complete cycle the change in internal energy is zero.
Enthalpy is internal energy plus pressure times volume.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of atoms and molecules that constantly move, vibrate or rotate. **Internal energy** is the sum of all the kinetic and potential energies of these particles. When a substance gets warmer, the particles move faster and the internal energy rises. Its symbol is usually U, and it is measured in joules.

In an ideal gas the particles do not attract each other, so only their movement counts. That is why, for a fixed amount of substance, internal energy depends only on **temperature**. For a monatomic gas such as helium it is three halves times amount of substance times gas constant times temperature. For one mole at 300 kelvin that is about 3.7 kilojoules, and if you heat 2 moles by 10 kelvin, the internal energy rises by about 249 joules.

A **degree of freedom** is an independent way in which a particle can move. A single atom can move in three directions and has 3 degrees of freedom. A diatomic molecule such as nitrogen can also rotate about two axes and has 5 degrees of freedom at room temperature. According to the **equipartition theorem**, each degree of freedom gets on average one half k times T, where k is the Boltzmann constant.

The **first law of thermodynamics** says that internal energy changes only when heat is added or work is done. When you rub your hands, work is turned into internal energy and your hands get warm. When you pump up a bike tyre, the pump gets warm because you are doing work on the gas. If a gas in an engine goes through a complete **cycle**, it is back in its starting state at the end, and the change in internal energy is zero.

In the 19th century researchers such as Julius Robert Mayer, James Prescott Joule and Rudolf Clausius realised that heat is a form of energy. Joule showed with a paddle wheel in water that mechanical work warms the water. For processes at constant pressure, for example in chemistry, **enthalpy** is often used. It is internal energy plus pressure times volume.

begriffe.erklaerung: Unit of energy, named after James Prescott Joule.
Independent way in which a particle can move.
Process in which a system returns to its starting state.
Internal energy plus pressure times volume.

gewusst: Because of its enormous mass, an iceberg has more internal energy in total than a hot cup of tea.
According to quantum physics, even at absolute zero the particles would still have a small leftover energy.
The unit joule is named after a brewer who did physics in his spare time.

teile.einleitung: Infrared radiation is invisible light whose wavelength is longer than that of red light. We cannot see it, but we can feel it as warmth on our skin. Every warm body, including humans, constantly gives off infrared radiation.
wichtigste: Infrared radiation has longer wavelengths than red light.
It reaches up to a wavelength of about 1 millimetre.
On the skin you feel infrared radiation as warmth.
William Herschel discovered it in 1800 with a thermometer.
Remote controls and thermal imaging cameras use infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases hold back the infrared radiation from the Earth's surface in the atmosphere.
Rattlesnakes can sense infrared radiation with special pit organs.

abschnitte.text: Light is an electromagnetic wave, and colours differ in their **wavelength**. Red light has the longest wavelength we can see, about 780 nanometres.
