Beyond that begins **infrared radiation**, which reaches up to a wavelength of about 1 millimetre. The name means below red, because its frequency is lower than that of red light.

In 1800 the astronomer **William Herschel** split sunlight into its colours with a glass prism. He put thermometers in the different colours and found that it got warmer towards red. It was actually warmest next to the red light, where nothing could be seen at all. That is how he discovered invisible heat radiation.

Every body that is warmer than absolute zero gives off **thermal radiation**. At room temperature and body temperature it lies almost entirely in the infrared. Humans also constantly radiate infrared because of their body heat. About half of the energy from the Sun that reaches us is infrared radiation, which is why sunshine feels warm.

An ordinary **remote control** sends invisible infrared flashes to the television. A **thermal imaging camera** shows how much infrared radiation objects give off and so makes warm spots visible. It can be used to find heat leaks in houses, missing people at night or overheated parts of machines. The James Webb Space Telescope also observes space in the infrared and so sees through clouds of dust.

The Earth's surface is warmed by the Sun and gives the heat off again as infrared radiation. **Greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour hold back part of this radiation in the atmosphere. Without this natural greenhouse effect, the average temperature on Earth would be about minus 18 °C. More greenhouse gases from humans strengthen the effect and lead to global warming.

**Rattlesnakes** and other pit vipers have small pit organs between the eye and the nostril. With them they sense the infrared radiation of warm prey, even in complete darkness. Some boas and pythons can also sense heat. A few beetles even find forest fires with infrared sensors, because they lay their eggs in freshly burnt wood.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance from one wave crest to the next.
Radiation that every warm body gives off.
A camera that makes infrared radiation visible and so shows temperatures.
A gas in the air that holds back thermal radiation.
The division of light or radiation by wavelength.

gewusst: With a mobile phone camera you can often see the flashing of a remote control, which is invisible to our eyes.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be an icy planet.
Herschel had already discovered the planet Uranus in 1781, before he found infrared radiation.

teile.einleitung: Interference is the overlapping of two or more waves. When wave crests meet, they reinforce each other; when a crest meets a trough, they cancel each other out. This creates patterns in water, sound and light.
wichtigste: In interference the displacements of waves add up.
Two coherent waves reinforce each other most when the path difference is a whole number multiple of the wavelength.
With an odd multiple of half the wavelength, waves of equal strength cancel each other out.
For a stable pattern the waves must be coherent.
Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference with anti-noise.
Two notes of 440 and 444 hertz produce a beat of 4 hertz.
With two sources in phase in a ripple tank, the lines of cancellation lie on hyperbolas.
The energy does not disappear when waves cancel; it is redistributed to places of reinforcement.

abschnitte.text: If you throw two stones into a pond at the same time, two circular waves travel towards each other. Where two crests meet, a particularly high crest forms; this is called **constructive interference**. When a crest meets a trough, they cancel out; this is **destructive interference**. In a ripple tank with two sources in phase, the lines of cancellation lie on hyperbolas.

Whether waves reinforce or cancel depends on the **path difference**, in other words how much further one wave has to travel to a point than the other. If it is a whole number multiple of the wavelength, crest meets crest. If it is an odd multiple of half the wavelength, crest meets trough. If two loudspeakers in phase send out a note with a wavelength of 1 metre, you hear almost nothing at a spot with a path difference of 0.5 metres.

For a stable pattern to form, the waves must be **coherent**, meaning they vibrate in step. Two ordinary light bulbs are not coherent, which is why you see no interference fringes with them. Laser light, on the other hand, is very coherent. At the beginning of the 19th century the Englishman Thomas Young showed with the **double slit experiment** that light forms interference fringes and is therefore a wave.

Headphones with active **noise cancelling** pick up surrounding noise with microphones. Then they produce anti-noise in which crests and troughs are exactly swapped, and the noise largely cancels out. If two tuning forks of 440 and 444 hertz sound at the same time, the note swells and fades four times a second. Musicians use this **beat** when tuning their instruments.

With **interferometers** you can measure lengths extremely accurately, because even tiny shifts change the fringe pattern. In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley used one to try to measure the movement of the Earth through a supposed ether, and found none. In 2015 huge laser interferometers in the USA detected gravitational waves for the first time. By the way, no energy is lost in interference; it is only redistributed from the dark places to the bright ones.

begriffe.erklaerung: Difference in the distance two waves travel to the same point.
Waves vibrate in a fixed rhythm with each other.
Regular swelling and fading of a note when two almost equal frequencies sound together.
Measuring device that uses interference for precise measurements.

gewusst: In holograms on banknotes and identity cards, the image is stored as an interference pattern.
Gravitational wave detectors change the length of their arms, which are several kilometres long, by only a tiny fraction of an atomic nucleus.
Water waves in a harbour basin can also become especially high in some places because of interference.

teile.einleitung: The International System of Units, SI for short, sets out the units in which lengths, masses, times and other quantities are measured. Today it is used in almost every country in the world and in science. Thanks to it, a metre in Switzerland means exactly the same as in Japan or Brazil.
wichtigste: The abbreviation SI comes from French: Système international d'unités.
The system was officially given the name SI in 1960.
It is based on the Metre Convention of 1875, which Switzerland also signed.
There are seven base units, for example the metre, the kilogram and the second.
All other units are derived from the base units.
The SI is coherent: derived units are formed without extra number factors.
The litre is not an SI unit, but it is accepted for use with the SI.

abschnitte.text: The **International System of Units** is a system of units of measurement that is valid worldwide. The abbreviation SI comes from French and stands for Système international d'unités. In the past almost every region had its own measures, such as the ell, the foot or the pound, which were a little different everywhere. This led to quarrels and mistakes in trade, so people wanted the same measures for everyone.

At the end of the 18th century France introduced the metric system with the metre and the kilogram. In 1875, 17 states signed the **Metre Convention** in Paris, Switzerland among them. They founded the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres near Paris. In 1960 the system was officially named SI, and it has been developed further ever since.

The SI has seven **base units**: the metre for length, the kilogram for mass, the second for time, the ampere for electric current, the kelvin for temperature, the mole for amount of substance and the candela for luminous intensity. Since 2019 all seven have been defined by fixed constants of nature, for example the speed of light. Before that, the kilogram was still defined by a metal cylinder in Sèvres, the **International Prototype Kilogram**.

All other units are put together from the base units. The newton for force is kg·m/s², the coulomb for charge is A·s, and the pascal for pressure is kg/(m·s²). Because no extra number factors are needed, the SI is called **coherent**. Units such as the litre, minute, hour or degree Celsius are not SI units, but they may be used together with the SI.

For very large and very small values there are **prefixes** that are placed in front of the unit. Kilo means a thousand, as in kilometre, and milli means a thousandth, as in millimetre. Mega stands for a million, micro for a millionth. This makes it easy to give everything from tiny bacteria to huge distances.

In Switzerland the SI is required by law, for example in trade and on packaging. The **Federal Institute of Metrology** METAS in Wabern near Bern makes sure that measurements throughout the country are correct. It checks scales, petrol pumps and speed cameras, for example. Only a few countries, such as the USA, still mainly use other units like miles and pounds in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the seven basic units of the SI.
International treaty of 1875 on uniform measures.
Syllable such as kilo or milli that makes a unit bigger or smaller.
The science of accurate measurement.

gewusst: For decades the old prototype kilogram was kept in a safe under three glass bell jars.
In 1999 a NASA space probe to Mars was lost because one team calculated with American units and another with metric units.
The second is defined by the vibrations of caesium atoms, which are counted in atomic clocks.

teile.einleitung: An isochoric process is one in which a gas heats up or cools down while its volume stays the same. The gas is sealed in a rigid container. If you heat it, the pressure rises; if you cool it, the pressure falls.
wichtigste: In an isochoric process the volume stays constant.
The expansion work is zero.
The pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature in kelvin.
This law is often named after the French physicist Guillaume Amontons.
On a p-V diagram the process appears as a vertical line.
You must not throw aerosol cans into a fire, because the pressure rises sharply with temperature.
The gas thermometer uses the change in pressure of a sealed gas at constant volume.

abschnitte.text: The word **isochoric** comes from Greek and means equal space. In this process a gas is sealed in a container that cannot expand. Heat is added or removed, and pressure and temperature change as a result. But the volume always stays the same.

A gas consists of tiny particles that constantly fly around and hit the walls. These collisions create the **pressure**. When the gas is heated, the particles move faster. They therefore hit the wall more often and harder, and the pressure rises.

At constant volume the pressure is proportional to the **absolute temperature** in kelvin. This law is often named after Guillaume Amontons, who lived around 1700, and sometimes after Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. A gas at 100 kPa and 300 K has three times the pressure at 900 K, or 627 °C. A bike tyre at 200 kPa and 20 °C would have about 220 kPa at 50 °C if its volume stayed the same.

Because the volume does not change, the gas does no **expansion work**; it is zero. All the heat supplied therefore increases the internal energy and with it the temperature. On a **p-V diagram**, where pressure is plotted against volume, an isochoric process is a vertical line. Together with isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes, it forms one of the basic building blocks of thermodynamics.

An **aerosol can** is a rigid container holding gas under pressure. If you throw it into a fire, the pressure rises sharply until the can may burst. That is also why gas cylinders must not stand in full sunshine or next to heaters. In a car engine the petrol and air mixture burns so quickly that in theory this step is treated as isochoric.

A **gas thermometer** measures temperature through the pressure of a sealed gas at constant volume. Because gases behave very evenly, such thermometers are very accurate. With their help people realised that the pressure of a gas would have to become zero at about minus 273 °C. This led to the idea of **absolute zero**, where the kelvin scale begins.

begriffe.erklaerung: At constant volume.
Temperature in kelvin, measured from absolute zero.
Work that a gas does when it expands or is compressed.
A diagram that shows the pressure of a gas against its volume.
The energy contained in the movement of the particles of a substance.

gewusst: A car tyre has a higher pressure after a long drive, because the air inside has warmed up.
A pressure cooker is almost an isochoric container, which is why the pressure rises when it is heated and water only boils above 100 °C.
At absolute zero, minus 273.15 °C, the particles of a gas would almost completely stop moving.

teile.einleitung: Infrasound is sound with such low notes that humans can no longer hear it. It lies below about 20 hertz. Elephants and whales communicate with it, and volcanoes or earthquakes produce it in large amounts.
wichtigste: Infrasound has a frequency below about 20 hertz.
Low notes are hardly absorbed by the air and therefore travel particularly far.
Elephants also communicate with infrasound over several kilometres.
The blue whale makes very low sounds, some of which are in the infrasound range.
Volcanic eruptions produce strong infrasound.
Humans perceive very strong infrasound as pressure or vibration.
Infrasound monitoring stations around the world check whether nuclear weapons are being tested in the air.
An infrasound note of 10 hertz has a wavelength of 34 metres in air.

abschnitte.text: Sound consists of pressure waves, and the number of vibrations per second is called the **frequency**. Humans hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz. Everything below about 20 hertz is called **infrasound**, everything above 20,000 hertz ultrasound. Infra comes from Latin and means below.

Because the vibrations are so slow, the waves are very long. A note of 10 hertz has a **wavelength** of 34 metres at a speed of sound of 340 metres per second, as long as a swimming pool with a diving tower. The air hardly absorbs such low notes, which is why infrasound travels hundreds or even thousands of kilometres. Walls and hills do not stop it well either.

**Elephants** make deep rumbling sounds, some of which lie in the infrasound range. Other elephants pick up these sounds over several kilometres, partly even through their feet as vibrations in the ground. The **blue whale**, the largest animal on Earth, also makes very low sounds that spread far through the sea. Researchers suspect that some birds also use infrasound to find their way.

Volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, avalanches, thunderstorms and strong storms produce powerful infrasound. When Krakatoa in Indonesia erupted in 1883, the pressure wave travelled round the whole Earth several times. Sea waves and wind over mountain ridges also produce a constant, quiet infrasound noise. Measuring instruments can even use it to detect avalanches in the Alps.

The organisation that monitors the **Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty**, based in Vienna, runs infrasound monitoring stations around the world. They are meant to detect nuclear weapons tests in the air, because an explosion produces a strong infrasound wave. The same stations also record meteors that explode in the atmosphere. Humans perceive very strong infrasound as pressure on the ears or as vibration in the stomach, even though they cannot hear it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
Distance from one wave crest to the next.
Sound that is too high for the human ear.
International agreement that bans all nuclear weapons tests.

gewusst: The pressure wave of the Krakatoa volcano was recorded on barometers around the world in 1883.
Large organs have pipes whose lowest notes are almost in the infrasound range and are felt rather than heard.
The Chelyabinsk meteor in 2013 was recorded by infrasound stations all over the world.

teile.einleitung: The gravitational constant G is a constant of nature that shows how strongly two masses attract each other. It appears in Newton's law of gravitation and has the same value everywhere in the universe. Its value is so tiny that we do not notice the attraction between everyday objects.
wichtigste: The gravitational constant G has a value of about 6.67·10^-11 m³/(kg·s²).
It appears in Isaac Newton's law of gravitation.
Two masses of 1 kg each, 1 m apart, attract each other with only about 6.7·10^-11 N.
G is the same everywhere in the universe, whereas the acceleration due to gravity g depends on the body in space.
In 1798 Henry Cavendish was the first to determine the attraction between masses in the laboratory.
With G you can calculate the mass of the Earth and of other bodies in space.
Compared with other constants of nature, G is known only relatively imprecisely.

abschnitte.text: Newton's **law of gravitation** says that the force between two masses is F = G·m1·m2/r². Here m1 and m2 are the masses and r is the distance between their centres. The number G turns this formula into a real force in newtons. Its value is about 6.674·10^-11, and its SI unit is m³/(kg·s²). That is a zero, a decimal point and then ten more zeros before the first digit 6.

Two masses of 1 kg each that are 1 m apart attract each other with about 6.7·10^-11 newtons. That is much less than the weight of a speck of dust. Two lead balls of 100 kg each, whose centres are 0.5 m apart, attract each other with about 2.7·10^-6 N. Only with huge masses such as planets and stars does **gravitation** become the deciding force. It keeps the Earth, for example, in its orbit around the Sun.

The big **gravitational constant G** and the small **acceleration due to gravity g** are often confused. G is a constant of nature and is the same everywhere, whether in Zurich, on Mars or in a distant galaxy. The acceleration due to gravity g is about 9.81 m/s² on Earth and only about 1.6 m/s² on the Moon. It depends on the mass and radius of the body in space. If you know g, the Earth's radius R and G, you can calculate the Earth's mass with M = g·R²/G; it is about 6·10^24 kg.

Newton knew the law, but not the value of G. In 1798 the English researcher **Henry Cavendish** built a sensitive **torsion balance**. Two small lead balls hung from a thin wire, and large lead balls next to them pulled them very slightly. From the tiny twist of the wire, the force of attraction could be determined. Because this made it possible to calculate the mass of the Earth, the experiment was also called “weighing the Earth”.

abschnitte.titel: Why G is hard to measure
abschnitte.text: Gravitation is the weakest of the four fundamental forces of nature. Between two protons it is about 10^36 times weaker than their electrical repulsion. That is why even the smallest influences such as air currents or vibrations disturb measurements. Other **constants of nature** such as the speed of light are known much more precisely than G. Researchers all over the world, including at Swiss universities, have measured G again and again with new methods.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number in physics that never changes and is the same everywhere.
Newton's rule for how strongly two masses attract each other.
A measuring device in which a thin wire is twisted by the tiniest forces.
One of the four basic forces of nature, such as gravitation or electromagnetism.

gewusst: You and your desk really do attract each other, but this force is far too weak to feel.
Cavendish actually wanted to determine the density of the Earth and found that it is about 5.5 times as dense as water.
Although gravitation is the weakest fundamental force, it shapes planets, stars and whole galaxies.
